claim: Track GMROI, gross margin dollars divided by inventory cost dollars, as the ROAS of your warehouse; Blue Sense's example brand earned 3.26 per dollar of stock, alongside turns (COGS divided by inventory).
body: Inventory usually takes more of a DTC brand's cash than any ad account, yet most operators watch ROAS daily and stock returns rarely. Gross margin return on inventory investment (GMROI) fixes that: gross margin dollars over a period divided by the average cost of inventory held. In the example, each dollar of stock produced 3.26 dollars of gross margin. Pair it with inventory turns (cost of goods sold divided by average inventory), which says how many times a year you sell through your stock. How to apply: compute both at the brand level and, more usefully, by category or SKU group, using landed cost and gross margin after fulfilment if you can. Rank SKUs by GMROI: low GMROI lines are tying up cash for little return and are candidates to buy less of, mark down or drop; high GMROI lines deserve stock priority and ad budget. Watch the trend: GMROI falls when gross margin drops (freight, FX, discounting) or when you hold more stock relative to sales (longer lead times).

claim: When a month misses plan, split the gap into order volume and average order value, then into new versus returning orders; Blue Sense's $120K miss was $70K volume and $50K AOV, all from new customers.
body: A miss is not just a soft month until you know where it came from. Blue Sense's example: the plan was $1.6 million, actual revenue $1.48 million, a $120,000 gap. Splitting it showed about $70,000 from fewer orders and about $50,000 from a lower average order value. Splitting orders by customer type showed returning customers hit plan while new customers fell short. So the problem was acquisition plus a discount mix that compressed order value, which points to specific fixes rather than a general push. How to apply: each month compute volume variance (order shortfall times planned AOV) and AOV variance (actual orders times the AOV gap), so they add to the total miss. Split planned and actual orders into new and returning. Then dig into the weak piece: for AOV, check units per order and average unit price, and the share of discounted orders; for new orders, check spend, cost per new customer and conversion rate. Bring the result to the weekly finance meeting and adjust spend, offers or stock buys.

claim: When deciding whether extra cash should go to Meta, value it at the marginal return of the next dollar (for example 2.7x), not the blended return (4x), or ads will always look like the best option.
body: Blended efficiency averages all your spend, including the cheapest, best-performing dollars. The next $100,000 lands at the top of the spend curve, where returns are lower. Blue Sense's example: a brand at a 25% MER (4x) should not expect $400,000 of revenue from another $100,000. Its marginal return might be 2.7x: $270,000 of revenue, about $150,000 of gross margin, and once the $100,000 of spend comes off, roughly $43,000 to $50,000 of contribution. Allbirds made the same point in its public filings, warning that marketing was getting more expensive and that added revenue might not cover added spend. How to apply: ask your agency or in-house team to model diminishing returns (plot daily spend against acquisition MER, fit a curve, read the slope at the planned level) and use acquisition MER rather than blended MER. Then compare that marginal contribution with paying down debt or buying stock. Blue Sense's warning: on blended numbers, more Meta spend nearly always wins in the short term; on marginal numbers, a certain and fast return such as debt paydown or a fast-selling reorder often beats it.
conditions: Brands spending enough on Meta for diminishing returns to show, typically five figures a month or more, with other uses for the cash.
fails_when: Small accounts far below their spend ceiling, where marginal and blended returns are close; or no curve has been modelled, so the marginal figure is a guess.

claim: When the 13-week cash forecast dips below your cash floor, fix it with supplier timing first (move or split the PO, net 60, a second supplier), then a short facility draw, and cut ad spend last.
body: The value of a 13-week view is warning time. In Blue Sense's example the forecast showed the bank balance falling under a $500,000 floor in week 10, which left about two and a half months to act. Their order of fixes: 1) ask the manufacturer to push the week-10 balance payment back about three weeks, or split it into two payments; 2) negotiate net 60 terms with that supplier for good, or use the runway to place the order with a second supplier on better terms; 3) draw on a finance facility for the few weeks of the gap, where interest of roughly $5,000 to $10,000 is a fair price for keeping the floor intact; 4) only then touch ad spend. Stock and ads were the two biggest cash lines, with ads at about 20 to 25% of revenue, but ad spend is what produces the payouts, so cutting it lowers revenue in the same weeks and can deepen the hole. In the example the gap was about $150,000 against roughly $100,000 a week of ads, so trimming would have meant about $30,000 off every week in the run-up to Black Friday. Blue Sense says weaker CFOs reach for a 30% marketing cut first. If ads must give, cut only a clearly wasteful top slice, such as the last $20,000 of a $100,000 week. A four or eight-week forecast would have spotted the problem too late to renegotiate the purchase order.

claim: Any single ecommerce metric can be gamed (pause cold ads and conversion rate jumps overnight), so set targets on LTGP to CAC, contribution profit and acquisition MER instead.
body: Blue Sense tells clients who ask only for higher conversion rate that it can be done in a day: switch off Facebook prospecting, cold traffic drops to zero, only warm buyers remain and the rate soars while an eight-figure brand loses millions. The same trick exists for every metric. Run traffic campaigns and sessions rise with no sales. Push expensive products and AOV rises even when their CAC makes them unprofitable. Quadruple spend and total sales rise while profit falls. How to apply: when you brief an agency, a freelancer or your own team, never give them one top-line metric. Give them a profit metric (contribution profit, LTGP to CAC on a fixed window, acquisition MER) and treat conversion rate, sessions, AOV and ROAS as diagnostics that explain movement in the profit number. If someone reports a win on a diagnostic, ask what happened to contribution profit in the same period.

claim: Blended conversion rate falls as you scale cold traffic: a site at 2.8% blended may be 1% on cold Meta and 4% on warm traffic, so a falling rate while scaling is expected.
body: Warm visitors (past buyers, email clicks, branded search) always convert better than strangers from a Meta ad. Your blended rate is a weighted average of the two, so the more of your traffic comes from cold Meta, the closer the blend sinks toward the cold rate. In the Blue Sense worked example, a store blends 2.8%, cold Meta converts at 1% and warm high-intent traffic at 4%. Turn Meta off and the rate jumps to about 4% overnight, while revenue collapses. This is why large brands with heavy cold spend often show low conversion rates, and why a high returning-customer share pushes both conversion rate and AOV up (returning AOV is usually higher than new). How to apply: before reacting to a conversion rate drop, split sessions and orders by new versus returning and by channel (GA4 or Shopify reports). If the cold-traffic share rose and cold conversion held, nothing is broken. Only treat it as a page problem when the rate drops inside the same traffic segment. Never set a team target on blended conversion rate during a scaling push.
conditions: Brands that run cold prospecting on Meta or TikTok alongside warm traffic from email, SMS, search and repeat buyers.
fails_when: Traffic is almost all from one source (for example only Google Shopping), so the mix barely moves and blended rate tracks page quality more closely.

claim: Judge site performance on revenue per visitor (conversion rate times AOV including shipping) or gross profit per visitor, tracked over about 2.5 years, not on conversion rate.
body: Conversion rate on its own says nothing about money. Blue Sense contrasts a store converting at 9% on a $45 to $55 impulse product that can only make Google work, with a brand converting at 1% that does $200 million online at a 50% contribution margin; the second is the far better business. Revenue per visitor (RPV) ties the page to revenue: multiply conversion rate by average order value, or divide sales by sessions. A step closer to profit is gross profit per visitor: multiply RPV by your gross margin percentage. Blue Sense says you could also take off ad costs, but they keep it simple and stop at gross profit. How to use it: pull monthly RPV for the last two to three years and look at the trend line. If RPV is rising, the site and offer are getting better at turning visits into money, even if blended conversion rate fell because you scaled cold traffic. If RPV is flat after a year of page tests, the tests did not matter. Use RPV, not conversion rate, as the success metric for any page, offer or checkout change, and when comparing yourself with other brands, compare nothing at all: their mix of traffic, price and category differs.
conditions: Any store running paid traffic where the mix of cold and warm visitors shifts over time; most useful once you have at least a year of session and order history.
fails_when: Session counts are polluted by bots or traffic campaigns, which drags RPV down for reasons unrelated to the page; fix the session source first. A very short window also misleads because of seasonality.

claim: Shopify's dashboard skews RPV maths: build revenue as net sales plus shipping collected (total sales includes tax, AOV excludes shipping) and take sessions from GA4, not Shopify.
body: Every input to conversion rate and revenue per visitor is a little wrong in the default Shopify view. Total sales includes tax, which is not your revenue, so either subtract tax or do what Blue Sense does: start from net sales and add back shipping collected. Shipping collected is real money taken at checkout, yet Shopify's average order value leaves it out, so AOV times conversion rate understates RPV. Sessions are the other weak spot: Shopify counts a lot of bot traffic, while GA4 filters bots better, so use GA4 sessions as the denominator whenever you divide by sessions. How to apply: in a sheet, set revenue = net sales + shipping collected for the period, sessions = GA4 sessions for the same period, then RPV = revenue / sessions. Recompute AOV the same way if you use the conversion rate times AOV route. Keep the method fixed so trends are comparable month to month.
conditions: Shopify stores that charge any shipping or collect tax at checkout, and that have GA4 installed.
fails_when: GA4 is badly installed or blocked by consent settings, so its sessions undercount more than Shopify overcounts; check both against each other first.

claim: Buy server-side tracking only if the few thousand dollars a month is easily affordable; Blue Sense has repeatedly failed to measure its lift because the effect is smaller than week-to-week noise.
body: Server-side tracking tools are sold hard on the signal quality argument. Blue Sense agrees better signal probably helps, but says the effect is very hard to see in results. When they introduce such a tool, the change is buried in normal weekly swings in revenue and ROAS. Comparing the 10 days before and after, or 30 and 30, or year on year, cannot separate it from everything else that changed at the same time, and even causal impact modelling lacks the variance to reach statistical confidence because the true effect is small. So a tool costing a couple of thousand dollars a month will probably not show a visible jump in efficiency. Their advice: if you can comfortably add it to the P&L and accept a hopeful, unproven upside, install it; if you need it to pay for itself in measurable results, do not expect that. Spend the effort on first-order economics and creative diversity first.
conditions: Brands deciding whether to pay for a third-party server-side tracking tool on top of native Conversions API.
fails_when: Setups where tracking is clearly broken (purchases missing in Events Manager), where fixing it gives a large and visible improvement.

claim: Your sustainable bid is your unit economics: brands with higher prices, gross profit, AOV and LTV win more auctions even with worse creative, so lifting first-order profit (upsells, better offers) beats any EMQ fix.
body: The part of the auction most people skip is that the bid itself comes from the business. The more margin you can afford to spend on acquiring a customer, the higher you can bid sustainably, the more auctions you win and the further you can scale. Competitors with higher prices, lower cost of goods, larger orders and better repeat rates can run weaker creative, messier structure and poorer measurement and still beat you, simply by outbidding you. Blue Sense puts it bluntly: you cannot out-tactic bad economics. That is why their audits start at the economic level and the whole team is trained in finance. How to apply: review first-order unit economics (AOV, gross margin, units per transaction, average unit retail) and 365-day lifetime gross profit; then raise first-order gross profit with post-purchase upsells, bundles and a better structured offer. They rate this as far more leverage than signal tweaks such as event match quality.
conditions: Any brand buying traffic in competitive Meta or Google auctions.
fails_when: Brands whose problem is creative or tracking failure so severe that even good margins cannot be spent profitably; fix those first.

claim: A brand dashboard needs only a few numbers: new customer profit contribution as the headline, then acquisition MER and new customer revenue, new customer orders, CAC and total profit contribution.
body: Blue Sense's recommended dashboard keeps volume and efficiency apart and ties both to profit. Headline: new customer profit contribution (new customer revenue minus the cost of delivering those orders minus marketing spend), which tells you if acquisition itself is profitable. Next to it: acquisition MER (efficiency, and it already reflects average order value) and new customer revenue (volume). Below: new customer orders, because revenue can move with order value while order count shows true volume; CAC (ad spend divided by new customers), a leading indicator that flags product mix or price shifts even when acquisition MER is steady; and total profit contribution. These come from Shopify and the P&L, not the ad platforms, so they are accurate. Track them daily or weekly to see whether last week's decisions helped. How to apply: tag COGS on every Shopify product so margins are real, build a sheet or BI view with these fields, and resist adding more. Once you pass high eight figures with heavy influencer, retail or other channel spend, add omnichannel revenue and incrementality factors, because even finance metrics then overstate one channel's role.
conditions: DTC brands with a Shopify store and paid acquisition; works from about $1M revenue up.
fails_when: Brands with large retail or wholesale revenue, where online new customer numbers miss much of the effect of ads.
numbers: profit contribution = revenue minus cost of delivery minus marketing

claim: A new upper funnel channel lifts ROAS elsewhere: Blue Sense saw TikTok report 1 to 2x while Meta mid funnel jumped from 4x to 12x, so cutting TikTok on its own ROAS removes the cause.
body: Upper funnel channels often under-report. On TikTok people watch, rarely click out, or view the product page and leave. Once they are in your Meta pixel, Meta retargets and closes the sale, and those who still have not bought later search your brand name on Google. So when TikTok spend goes up, Meta ROAS and Google ROAS go up while TikTok's own ROAS stays low. Blue Sense describes a test where TikTok ran at about 25% of the Meta budget, reported only 1x to 2x, and at the same time the Meta middle funnel campaign jumped from 4x to 12x. A team reading platform ROAS would cut TikTok, raise Meta budgets (even on cold campaigns, wrongly assuming Meta itself improved), and push more into Google, which removes the very spend that created the demand. Blue Sense reports seeing this pattern with some large retail brands in 2026. How to apply: when a channel is added or cut, watch the other channels' ROAS shift in the same weeks and judge the whole system on new customer revenue and acquisition MER. If a channel looks weak in platform but others jump when it runs, test it with a holdout or geo split before deciding.
conditions: Brands running Meta plus at least one other upper funnel channel (TikTok, YouTube, influencers) and a branded search campaign.
fails_when: Channels launched at a spend too small to move anything, or periods where a promotion or season explains the jump instead.

claim: Allocate budget by next best dollar: put each extra $10,000 where it returns the most new customer revenue, keep raising a channel until its marginal acquisition MER hits break-even, and add channels only after the main ones reach that point.
body: Blue Sense says every founder or head of marketing should be able to answer one question: if we spent an extra $10,000 next month, where would it go and what would it return? Most cannot answer reliably, so they push spend up everywhere and wonder why returns fade. The frame is the profit frontier. For each channel (for example Meta at $100,000, Google at $50,000, TikTok at $70,000), estimate the new customer revenue an extra $10,000 would produce. Also ask the reverse: could $10,000 pulled from Google, returning 2x on new customer revenue, earn 4x in Meta? Keep moving money toward the best marginal return, and keep raising a channel until the last dollar only breaks even on acquisition MER; past that, more spend loses money. Only once Meta, Google and TikTok are all at that frontier should you add new channels. How to apply: the reliable way to read marginal returns is controlled incrementality tests on budget steps; smaller brands can approximate with their own spend versus acquisition MER curves per channel or a marketing mix model, plus a good buyer's judgement.
conditions: Brands spending on two or more channels with some way to read marginal returns.
fails_when: Single-channel accounts; or when measurement is attribution-only, which will bias the frontier toward bottom funnel channels.

claim: Around March or April 2026 Meta narrowed 7-day click to outbound clicks only and moved likes, comments, shares and profile clicks into 1-day engaged, so click-only ROAS dropped overnight.
body: Before the change, Meta's click window counted any click on the ad unit, not just a click through to your website. Liking, commenting, sharing or tapping the page name all counted as a click, so a person could comment on an ad, buy days later, and Meta would book it as a click conversion. Few advertisers knew this. Meta then rewrote the definition so 7-day click means an outbound click to the site. Those engagement interactions now sit in a separate 1-day engaged bucket. Two practical effects: first, any 7-day click ROAS trend line has a step down at the change date that is not a real performance drop, so do not compare click-only results before and after it without noting the break. Second, include 1-day engaged in your setting, because a person who engaged with an ad and then bought within a day likely has some real causal link, and it holds what used to be called a click. Blue Sense recommends 7-day click plus 1-day engaged as the default and dropping plain 1-day view.
conditions: Meta advertisers comparing 2026 attribution data with earlier periods; the change was described as of May 2026.
fails_when: Meta changes definitions often; check the current definition in Ads Manager before relying on this.

claim: Back-solve a contribution margin target from your net profit goal: a 20% net target with opex at 15% needs 35% contribution margin; $1M net plus $1M opex needs $2M contribution.
body: Contribution margin (often labelled CM3) is revenue minus cost of delivery minus all marketing. Blue Sense likes it because it sits one step above net profit: subtract opex and you have EBITDA. Since opex should be fairly stable, a contribution target set high in the P&L guarantees the bottom line. Percent example: target 20% net profit, opex holds at 15%, so contribution must reach 35%. Dollar example: target $1M net profit, opex $1M, so the year needs $2M of contribution. Simple waterfall: revenue 100%, cost of delivery 30%, marketing 20%, so contribution is 50%; minus opex 10% gives 40%. Watch naming: some people say contribution margin meaning CM1 (product margin) or CM2 (gross margin after all variable delivery costs), so confirm which one an agency or CFO means before agreeing on a target. How to apply: set the annual net profit goal, add forecast opex, convert to a contribution target, then work out the marketing ratio that hits it at your gross margin. Give that contribution target to the marketing team or agency instead of a ROAS target.
conditions: Brands with stable, known opex and accurate gross margin.
fails_when: Periods of planned opex jumps (new warehouse, big hires), when the target must be recalculated.
numbers: 20% net + 15% opex = 35% contribution target
$1M net + $1M opex = $2M contribution

claim: Benchmark 180-day LTGP to CAC: under 1 is dangerous (payback over 6 months), 1 to 2 is okay, 2 to 3 is the zone to scale, and over 3 means you are underspending.
body: LTGP to CAC is gross profit a customer generates in a fixed window divided by the cost to acquire them. Because it is a ratio of two paired numbers, it can be compared across time and across very different businesses, which acquisition MER cannot: a 4x acquisition MER is great for one brand and terrible for another depending on margin and other channel spend. Blue Sense uses it to rank its whole client book. Benchmarks on a 180-day window: below 1 means you have not earned back acquisition cost in 6 months; unless heavily funded this is a high risk position that forces you to float capital. 1 to 2 is profitable on acquisition but inefficient, so either CAC is too high or gross profit per customer too low. 2 to 3 is where Blue Sense looks to increase spend. Above 3 is also a mistake: you are leaving growth on the table and should push spend harder, unless cash flow is the limit, in which case fix cash flow rather than borrow heavily. Quick check from part 2 of the video: to sit at 2, CAC must be no more than first order gross profit divided by 2, so $100 gross profit allows a $50 CAC.
conditions: Brands with accurate COGS and cohort data; gross profit must use true cost of delivery, not product margin.
fails_when: Venture funded brands deliberately buying growth below 1, or subscription models with proven long retention; the 180-day window flatters brands with long repeat cycles less.

1 to 2: okay
2 to 3: scale

claim: Blue Sense's nine recurring audit findings: 1-day view in reporting, Google halo, brand search waste, over-segmentation, tiny tertiary channels, existing customer overspend, unmeasured traffic or reach campaigns, DPA overspend and no testing structure.
body: Use this as a checklist when auditing an account. 1) 1-day view running and used in reporting, with 30 to 50% of ROAS coming from view-throughs. 2) Google halo: Google claims credit for demand built elsewhere, so its ROAS looks better than its real effect. 3) Brand search waste: brand terms left in campaigns to lift ROAS, common even at large eight and nine figure retailers. 4) Over-segmentation: too many campaigns for the spend or business complexity, which splits data and makes decisions muddled. 5) Tertiary channels such as Snapchat, Pinterest or Reddit at low spend; at low budgets they mostly serve warm site visitors and report high ROAS while adding no new customers. 6) Existing customer overspend, raised because its ROAS looks good. 7) Traffic or reach campaigns with no way to measure them. 8) Overspend on DPAs, which sit at the bottom of the funnel. 9) No testing or experiment structure, so nobody knows if anything new works. How to apply: walk the account in this order, quantify each issue in spend, and fix the measurement items (1, 6, 8) first because they distort every other decision.
conditions: Meta and Google accounts of brands at roughly $5M+ revenue; findings come from Blue Sense's audit practice.
fails_when: Accounts already reporting on 7-day click with existing customers excluded and incrementality tests in place.

claim: CAC is total ad spend divided by new customers in the period; dividing by all orders gives blended CPA, which looks cheaper because repeat orders cost little, and channel-level CAC cannot be measured reliably.
body: Blue Sense says most brands calculate CAC wrongly. True customer acquisition cost is total advertising spend over a period (day, week or month) divided by the number of first-time customers in that period. Many brands instead divide spend by all orders, which mixes in repeat buyers who cost almost nothing to bring back, so CAC looks lower than it is and budgets get scaled on a false picture. CAC is also not the platform's CPA, which runs on attributed conversions and will usually look better than the business reality. Trying to compute CAC per channel runs into the same attribution problem, so Blue Sense treats it as a business level number. How to apply: pull new customer count from Shopify (customers whose first order falls in the period) and total ad spend across all platforms, and track that ratio as your CAC. Watch it alongside acquisition MER: acquisition MER captures order value and is the better profit read, while CAC moving on its own is an early warning that product mix, pricing or the new customer offer has shifted.
conditions: Any brand with repeat purchasing; data from Shopify or the order system.
fails_when: Stores with almost no repeat buyers, where blended and true CAC are close.

claim: Calculate LTV as gross profit, not revenue, over a capped window such as 90 or 180 days; many tools report LTV as revenue over all time, which keeps rising and justifies overspending.
body: Two common LTV errors. First, no time limit: measured across all history, lifetime value keeps climbing (for example $100 at 6 months, $110 at 12, $120 at 18) even though it flattens, so any acquisition cost can be justified on paper while the cash takes years to return. Second, revenue instead of profit: the LTV idea came from software, where lifetime revenue and lifetime gross profit are nearly the same because delivery costs are tiny. In ecommerce they are very different, yet many apps still show LTV as revenue. Blue Sense uses lifetime gross profit (LTGP) over 90 or 180 days and compares that with CAC to decide what it can pay for a customer. How to apply: in your cohort report, sum gross profit per first-order cohort at 90 and 180 days using true cost of delivery, divide by cohort size, and use that, not app-reported LTV, for any CAC ceiling or decision to lose money on first orders. Check the window against your cash cycle, because cash spent on acquisition today competes with inventory you must buy now.
conditions: Brands with repeat purchasing using LTV to justify acquisition spend.
fails_when: Subscription brands with long proven retention and cheap capital, which may use longer windows deliberately.
numbers: example LTV $100 at 6 months, $110 at 12, $120 at 18

claim: Do not make decisions from Shopify's marketing attribution reports or GA4; keep GA4 set up only as a backup in case platform tracking fails, and make sure Meta CAPI is firing.
body: Blue Sense's tracking advice for brands of $10M to $20M is short. First, Meta Conversions API must work: purchase events go from your server to Meta rather than only from the browser pixel, which ad blockers and iOS privacy settings weaken. CAPI also passes hashed email, phone and customer ID, which lifts match rates, and allows offline or in-store sales with an email or phone to be matched back to ads. Second, ignore Shopify's marketing and attribution reports; Blue Sense has found little useful in them. Third, treat GA4 as a redundancy layer, not a decision dashboard, because there is little in it you cannot get from Shopify or the ad platforms. Keep it configured properly (events firing, campaign segmentation through UTMs) so that if a platform's tracking breaks you have clean history to fall back on for direction. How to apply: check CAPI in Events Manager (event match quality and deduplication), check GA4 is collecting purchases with UTMs, then make weekly decisions from Shopify order data, the P&L and in-platform data on fixed attribution settings.
conditions: Shopify brands with paid media; view as of May 2026.
fails_when: Stores without server-side tracking where GA4 may be the only cross-channel view; brands whose analytics team has built a trusted GA4 model.
numbers: advice aimed at brands doing $10M to $20M+ revenue

claim: Existing customers inside cold campaigns inflate ROAS even on click-only attribution, because a repeat buyer clicking a reminder ad was usually going to reorder anyway.
body: Removing view-throughs does not remove all inflation. If past customers are not excluded from prospecting, they see and click your ads and buy again, and the platform books it as a click conversion. Blue Sense's example is a supplement buyer with five days left in the pack: the ad just nudged a purchase forward by a few days that was coming regardless. That sale is not new demand, so a cold campaign full of these orders reports a ROAS far above its real effect. The problem grows with business size: more customers means more chances for bleed. How to apply: upload or sync your customer list (Klaviyo or Shopify audiences) and set it up as Existing customers in Meta's audience segments so prospecting excludes or caps them. In Ads Manager use the Audience segments breakdown to see how much spend and revenue goes to new, engaged and existing people. Judge cold campaigns on new customer revenue and acquisition MER rather than attributed revenue. Check the sync often, because Blue Sense sees the Klaviyo to Meta sync break and quietly put existing customers back into new.
conditions: Brands with a meaningful customer base and repeat purchase; consumables and fashion especially.
fails_when: Stores with very few past customers, or one-time purchase categories where repeats are rare.
numbers: example: supplement buyer with 5 days left in the pack

claim: Fix measurement by subtracting, not adding: more attribution tools, dashboards and conversion events create conflicting reads; keep a short ranked list of commercial KPIs that decide every call.
body: Once teams learn platform ROAS is inflated, about half the market (by Blue Sense's estimate) responds by adding more: a third party attribution tool, extra dashboards, extra conversion events, more settings. The result is meetings where one person cites a multi-touch model saying Pinterest is bad, another cites an incrementality test saying it is good, and a third cites a causal model saying it is bad again. Nobody can decide. Blue Sense's rule is to strip data away and set a hierarchy: one or two metrics at the top that, if they are on target, settle the question, then supporting metrics below that explain why. A good metric changes your behaviour when you read it; if it does not, drop it. How to apply: write down the top metric (for most brands new customer profit contribution or acquisition MER), the two or three supporting metrics (new customer revenue, new customer orders, CAC), and which data source is the tiebreaker when two disagree. Document where each number comes from and how it is calculated, since a missing data governance note is another common audit finding.
conditions: Teams with several people or agencies reading different tools; brands of $5M+ with a C-suite reporting line.
fails_when: Very large multi-channel brands that genuinely need multi-source measurement, as long as it is organised into a hierarchy.

claim: Forecast new customer revenue by plotting a year of daily acquisition MER against spend, removing sale days and very low spend days, fitting a curve, and reading what spend hits your target.
body: For paid acquisition, Blue Sense builds a simple response curve. Put daily spend on the x axis and daily acquisition MER on the y axis for about the last year. Remove outliers that would distort normal trading: sale periods, Black Friday and November days, and days below a minimum spend you will never run at again. Fit a logarithmic or linear regression, whichever fits best. The line shows the efficiency to expect at each spend level, for example what acquisition MER $8,000 a day should deliver. Then work backward from the goal. If you want $100,000 of new customer revenue at a 4 acquisition MER, read where 4 sits on the curve and whether the spend at that point produces enough revenue. Often it does not, and that gap is the point of forecasting: the board wants $50M, the curve says $40M, so name the inputs that will close the $10M gap. Options include a new marketing event, product launches, a new channel, or a step change such as tripling creative output. How to apply: refresh the curve quarterly and record which input is expected to move it.
conditions: Brands with a year of fairly consistent daily spend; works best for paid-led acquisition.
fails_when: Brands with large influencer, retail or other channel effects, which need a fuller model; data spanning big structural changes.

claim: Forecast returning customer revenue from cohorts: apply each past cohort's expected repeat rate for its next month times returning AOV; it lands within about 10%, and about 1 to 2% once you add seasonality and planned events.
body: Blue Sense's first rule of ecommerce forecasting is to forecast new and returning customer revenue separately, because they have different drivers. New customers come mainly from paid ads, plus influencers and events. Returning customers come mainly from product launches, sale events, email and SMS and other reasons to come back. For returning revenue, use cohort maths. Take every monthly cohort of new customers back to the start (for example from January 2021). Each cohort repeats at a declining rate over time, something like 7% in month one, then 6%, 4%, 2%, 1%, flattening near a small number. For next month, multiply each cohort's size by the average repeat rate for the month of life it is about to enter (for example 0.1% in month 32) and by returning customer AOV. 100 customers times 0.1% times $100 gives $1. Sum across all cohorts. Blue Sense finds this lands within about 10%. To get within 1 to 2%, apply a seasonality factor from the last three years of returning revenue, then add expected revenue from any marketing event not run in the prior year.
conditions: Brands with at least 12 to 24 months of cohort history and steady repeat behaviour.
fails_when: Young brands with little cohort history, or after big changes to product range or retention programme.

claim: In Australia, state-level geo tests rarely work: there are too few states, you need huge spend, and back-to-back tests muddy the clustering; split the country into commuting zones instead.
body: Geo-lift testing depends on finding groups of regions that move together and can stand in for each other. The US has 50 states, which gives plenty of combinations. Australia has only a handful of states and territories, so finding a matched control is hard, a test needs very large spend to move a state's revenue, and running another test soon after disturbs the historical data used to pick regions, so tests cannot be stacked quickly. Blue Sense's fix is to run Australian geo tests at a commuting zone level: break the country into many smaller sub-regions based on where people live and work, which gives enough units to build matched control and treatment groups. How to apply: map orders and spend to postcode based commuting zones, run the same matching on spend, new customer revenue and new customer orders, and make sure ad delivery can be targeted to those zones. Leave gaps between tests so the next selection starts from clean data.
conditions: Australian brands, or any market with few large states, with enough spend to run geo tests.
fails_when: Markets with many comparable regions such as the US, where state-level designs work; brands too small to run geo tests at all.
numbers: Australia has too few states for clean state-level design

claim: In a typical $200k a month brand, returning customers can earn more profit than new ones (Blue Sense's example: $27.5k versus $20k), so acquisition profit should be tracked separately and LTV assumptions checked before subsidising new buyers.
body: Blue Sense's worked month: $200k revenue, of which $140k is new customer revenue driven by $50k of ad spend, and $60k is returning customer revenue costing about $2.5k (Klaviyo plus a retention agency). With a 50% gross margin, new customer gross profit is $70k, minus $50k ads, leaving $20k of new customer profit contribution. Returning revenue gives $30k gross profit, minus about $2.5k, leaving about $27.5k. So this fairly normal business makes more from returning buyers than new ones, because returning customers come back on product, experience and brand without much paid spend. That tempts brands to spend returning profit to push new customer acquisition harder. Blue Sense's warning: only do that with a correctly calculated LTV, because most brands overestimate it. How to apply: report new customer profit contribution and returning customer profit contribution as two lines each month; decide how much returning profit you are willing to reinvest in acquisition; and set that limit using a capped 90 or 180 day gross profit LTV, not lifetime revenue.
conditions: Brands with a meaningful returning share (roughly 25% to 40% of revenue) and low retention costs.
fails_when: One-time purchase categories where returning revenue is minimal.

claim: In over 1,000 Blue Sense audits, broken measurement was the main growth bottleneck in about 30% of businesses; fix the metrics before creative or account structure.
body: Blue Sense treats a store as three layers. Data integrity sits at the base, creative sits on top of it, and technical account structure sits on top of creative. Each layer only pays off if the one under it works. A clever account structure is wasted if the creative is weak, and both are wasted if the numbers used to judge them are wrong. The warning sign of bad data is a team that keeps analysing, iterating and launching, yet profit and revenue do not move. That treadmill feeling usually means the metric being optimised (often platform ROAS) is not tied to a real commercial outcome. Every scaling decision is a feedback loop: read a number, act, read again. If the first number is inflated, every later decision compounds the error, for example making more ads like a '4x' ad that was never driving new customers. How to apply: before rebuilding campaigns or briefing more creative, check that the team reports on numbers that reconcile to the P&L (new customer revenue, acquisition MER, contribution), that view-through and existing customer revenue are stripped out, and that tracking fires correctly. Then look for the next single bottleneck, solve it, and repeat, because growth comes from clearing one constraint after another.
conditions: Brands spending enough on paid media that decisions are made from platform dashboards; most true at $5M+ revenue where multiple channels muddy attribution.
fails_when: Very small single-channel stores where platform numbers are close to the truth; there the bottleneck is more often the product, offer or creative.

data integrity was the bottleneck in about 30% of them

claim: In-platform lift tests are fast and split users individually, but you cannot check the platform's maths, they still rely on its attribution, and TikTok and Google set high minimum spends (Blue Sense cites about $200,000 on TikTok).
body: Meta, Google and TikTok can run conversion lift studies. Because they know each user, they split people into exposed and held-out groups at the individual level rather than by region, then compare purchase rates seen by the pixel. Meta lets you run these fairly freely; Blue Sense says TikTok requires a minimum spend of about $200,000 for a test, and Google also needs large budgets. Pros: quick, can be repeated often, no regional design needed. Cons: you get no access to the raw data, so you trust the platform's data science without verification, and the result still depends on the pixel attributing purchases correctly. Geo-lift tests are the reverse: slow, expensive, require holding other variables steady across the test period, but every number is your own and can be checked, and they can include offline revenue. How to apply: use in-platform lift studies for frequent, faster checks on campaign types (for example how incremental DPAs or retargeting really are), and use geo-lift for the large decisions such as adding a channel or a big budget increase. Blue Sense recommends having both in the testing plan.
conditions: Brands spending enough to meet each platform's minimum; Meta tests are accessible at lower budgets than TikTok or Google.
fails_when: Small accounts below minimum spends; decisions that need offline or Amazon revenue, which pixel based tests do not see.

claim: Judge paid media on acquisition MER (new customer revenue divided by ad spend), not MER: Blue Sense sees blended MER rise from 4x to 5x while acquisition MER falls from 2 to 1.6, hiding loss-making scaling.
body: MER is total revenue divided by ad spend (or the reverse as a percentage; 20% and 5x are the same number). It is a good CFO metric because it shows what share of revenue goes to marketing, and with gross margin and opex under control it delivers a steady profit target. It is a bad metric for judging marketers, because most ad money buys new customers while total revenue includes returning buyers who would come back anyway. Blue Sense's audit pattern: January MER 4x, February 5x, so the team raises spend in March and MER settles back to target. Split it out and acquisition MER went 2, then 1.8, then 1.6: February's jump was returning customer revenue, new customer efficiency was falling, and each budget increase made acquisition less profitable unnoticed. How to apply: compute acquisition MER weekly from Shopify (first-time customer revenue, net of returns, divided by total ad spend). Use net revenue, not gross, especially in fashion where returns land later. Set the target from your own margin and retention: a 60% gross margin brand can live with a much lower acquisition MER than a 40% one, and strong repeat rates justify a more aggressive target, so never borrow another brand's number.
conditions: Brands with a meaningful share of returning customer revenue; anyone using MER to set budgets.
fails_when: Brands whose ads are deliberately aimed at reactivating existing customers, or very new stores where nearly all revenue is new anyway.

claim: Keep a fixed in-house creative team in opex and put flexible agency or short-term creative for peaks (in Australia, June end of financial year and November to December) in marketing, because it varies with revenue.
body: Creative production is the grey area in the P&L. Content volume needs to rise and fall with expected revenue. A typical Australian DTC year is flat in Q1, spikes in June for end of financial year sales, builds again, peaks in November and December, then drops. An in-house team sized for the average is under-used in quiet months and badly overloaded at peaks. Blue Sense's model is a fixed in-house core for the baseline content need, plus agencies or short-term contract hires for the peaks, often three months at a time. Account for them differently: the fixed in-house team is an ongoing cost held indefinitely, so it sits in operating expenses; the flexible agency and contract spend varies with revenue, so it belongs in the marketing line and counts toward MER, along with ads, influencers, events and outdoor. Some brands put all creative in marketing because it all drives revenue; that is a valid choice as long as it is consistent. How to apply: map monthly creative volume against your revenue curve, size the in-house team to the trough, and pre-book flexible capacity for the peaks.
conditions: DTC brands with seasonal peaks and paid social that depends on fresh creative; seasonal calendar given is Australian.
fails_when: Brands with flat year-round demand, where a fully in-house team fits.

claim: Keep opex nearly flat as revenue grows so profit margin expands; across about 300 seven-figure clients, founders usually let people, software and office costs rise faster, leaving profit flat for years.
body: An ecommerce P&L has three big cost buckets: cost of delivery and marketing, which rise with revenue, and operating expenses, which should stay roughly fixed because a store does not need many more people to sell more. If opex holds steady while revenue climbs, profit grows as a share of revenue. Blue Sense worked with nearly 300 seven-figure brands in its first four years and saw the opposite again and again: founders hire, add software and upgrade offices faster than marketing and delivery costs grow, so dollar profit stays flat while the business gets bigger and harder to run. Its point is that a $5M brand at 20% net profit ($1M) is a better asset than a $10M brand at 5% ($500k). The phrase 'reinvest in the business' should mean marketing, the main growth lever in ecommerce, not headcount, tools or space, which rarely drive revenue directly. People matter most, but small brands usually cannot attract or judge top talent yet. How to apply: track opex as a percentage of revenue monthly, set a ceiling (for example 10% to 15%), and require any new hire or tool to show how it raises revenue or cuts cost of delivery.
conditions: Seven and low eight figure DTC brands scaling mainly through paid media.
fails_when: Brands whose growth depends on product development, retail sales teams or in-house manufacturing, where some fixed costs do drive revenue.

claim: Match measurement to revenue: at $1M to $5M use 7-day click, tagged COGS and a daily new customer dashboard; at $5M to $20M add platform lift studies; past $20M run your own geo-lift tests.
body: Blue Sense's action plan by size. $1M to $5M a year: switch Meta reporting to 7-day click, which tracks acquisition MER much better; tag cost of goods on every Shopify product; build a daily dashboard showing new customer revenue and orders, acquisition MER, blended CAC, and both total and new customer profit contribution; exclude existing customers from top of funnel campaigns; keep brand search spend to a minimum. $5M to $20M: keep all of that, add in-platform lift studies, test top of funnel ideas measured by those studies, and use Meta's incremental attribution as a second check beyond 7-day click. $20M and up: the channel mix and the places revenue is captured get complex, so run geo-lift tests outside the platforms, pull omnichannel revenue (retail, marketplaces) into the dashboard, and add incrementality factors from your tests to the reported ROAS of each channel and campaign type. How to apply: place your brand on this ladder, finish the lower rungs before spending on the higher ones, and do not buy enterprise measurement before the basics reconcile.
conditions: DTC brands from about $1M revenue up; tiers reflect Blue Sense's client base in Australia and the US.
fails_when: Brands with unusual complexity early (big wholesale or retail at small online revenue), which may need higher-rung methods sooner.

claim: Meta's incremental attribution column is not a live holdout in your account; it applies a factor modeled from lift tests other advertisers in your niche ran, so treat it as a directional second read.
body: A conversion lift test holds out part of the audience (Meta uses about 10%) and compares purchase rates. If 2% of people who saw ads bought and 1% of the held out group still bought, ads caused only the 1 point difference, so a reported 5x ROAS is really about 2.5x. Known brands have a high baseline because people buy without ads; a $10,000 a month unknown store has a baseline near zero. Meta's incremental attribution setting, rolled out around late 2025, looks like this kind of read, but Blue Sense explains it is not running holdouts in your account in real time. Meta takes results from lift studies run by competitors in your niche and industry and applies a modeled factor to your conversions. How to apply: in Ads Manager open Columns, Compare attribution settings, and add incremental attribution next to 7-day click. Use it to rank campaign types (for example DPAs and retargeting usually shrink most) and as a second validation layer, not as audited truth. For budget calls above a few hundred thousand a month, back it with your own lift or geo tests.
conditions: Meta accounts where the setting is available; most useful for brands with existing awareness and many warm buyers.
fails_when: Unusual categories where competitors' lift tests do not reflect your buyers; very new brands where nearly all sales are already incremental.

claim: Never compare ROAS across platforms: Pinterest counts view-throughs and can claim a sale when any of 6 to 12 visible tiles was an ad, so a 7x Pinterest ROAS can be worth less than 2.5x on Meta.
body: Each platform uses its own attribution window and its own idea of an interaction, and each sits at a different point in the funnel. Pinterest is the extreme case Blue Sense describes. It includes view-through conversions, and a Pinterest feed shows roughly 6 to 12 tiles at once depending on screen size. If one of those tiles is your ad and the person later buys, Pinterest can claim the sale without a click. Low budget Pinterest delivery also tends to drift toward warm people who visited your site in the last few days and would have bought anyway. The result is a big reported ROAS, for example a 7 against Meta's 2.5, that tempts teams to move budget. Google uses longer click windows (often 30 days) plus view windows, and TV shows zero because nothing is attributed. How to apply: compare platforms only on numbers that sit outside the platforms (new customer revenue and acquisition MER over time, holdout or geo tests), and only compare ROAS between campaigns inside the same platform with the same attribution setting.
conditions: Brands running two or more paid platforms and allocating budget between them.
fails_when: Comparisons made on matched, click-only attribution with incrementality tests behind them.

claim: Offline activations, retail stores and organic reach lift digital ROAS in ways the ad account cannot see, and the inflation grows as a business matures, so a ROAS jump in one region may have nothing to do with the ads.
body: Blue Sense calls the third source of inflation the halo effect. A big retailer runs a pop-up in New York and ad performance in New York triples. Someone who only looks at the ad account sees a great week and pushes spend, but the lift came from an outside event, not the ads; it was correlation with a confounding cause. Mature businesses suffer this most because they have far more existing customers, more channels running at once (retail stores act like advertising simply by being there), and much larger organic reach. The bigger the brand, the less any attributed number at any level can be trusted on its own. How to apply: keep a shared calendar of every offline or off-platform activity (pop-ups, PR, retail openings, influencer drops, email launches) and annotate it against ad results before acting on a jump. Do not raise budgets in a region or week that coincides with such an event. As the brand passes eight figures, shift decision weight from attributed ROAS to finance numbers and to geo or holdout tests that control for these events.
conditions: Omnichannel brands, brands with retail stores, strong organic or PR, and anyone running several channels at once.
fails_when: Small single-channel online stores where nothing outside the ad account is happening.
numbers: example: pop-up in New York, ad account performance in New York tripled

claim: Profit is not cash: a brand showing $2M P&L profit that bought $3M of inventory that did not sell is about $1M cash negative, so read the balance sheet before scaling spend.
body: In ecommerce, growing means paying for future stock while also paying for ads today. So even a business showing $100k, $1M or $2M of profit may leave the founder no cash to take, because it all goes back into the next purchase orders. Blue Sense's example: the P&L shows $2M profit for the year, but the balance sheet holds $3M of unsold inventory bought that year. The cash went into stock that has not turned back into money, so the business is roughly $1M cash negative despite a profitable P&L. For most stores the balance sheet is mainly inventory and cash. This is why paid media in ecommerce is harder than in services, SaaS or info products: scaling ad spend only works if the inventory bought to support it sells through. How to apply: before approving a spend increase, review cash on hand, inventory value by sell-through grade, open purchase orders and their payment dates. Share that view with the marketing team or agency so their plans reflect cash, not just ROAS or P&L profit.
conditions: Inventory-holding brands, especially fast-growing ones with long supplier lead times.
fails_when: Print on demand, dropship or pre-order models that do not hold stock.

claim: Put warehouse pick-pack staff in cost of delivery as a per-order cost (for example $400 a day over 100 packages is $4 an order), and keep loan interest below EBITDA, never in opex.
body: Two classification mistakes Blue Sense sees on seven and eight figure P&Ls. First, warehouse staff who pick, pack and ship are a cost of fulfilling orders, like a 3PL fee, so they belong in cost of delivery, not operating expenses. Convert them to a per-order cost: a packer paid about $400 a day who ships about 100 orders a day adds about $4 per order. Your bookkeeper can tag those staff in the accounting software and produce a custom P&L that moves them into cost of delivery, so gross margin is accurate month by month. Opex then holds the people not tied to fulfilment (head of marketing, operations), software, and offices. Second, interest on inventory loans or other financing is not an operating expense. It is the cost of leverage used to grow faster. Put it below EBITDA: revenue, minus cost of delivery, marketing and opex gives EBITDA; minus interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation gives net profit. A buyer values the business on EBITDA because they would clear the loans, so interest in opex makes the business look less profitable than it is. Example: $20 EBITDA, $10 interest, $10 net profit.
conditions: Brands with in-house fulfilment staff or financing; anyone preparing for a sale or investor review.
fails_when: Brands fully outsourced to a 3PL with no debt, where these lines do not exist.

claim: ROAS gets more reliable as you move up the Meta structure: ad-level ROAS is weakest, ad set better, and campaign ROAS on 7-day click with existing customers excluded tracks the P&L closely.
body: Campaigns set budget and the optimisation event, ad sets hold the targeting (even with broad audiences, delivery decisions sit there), and ads are the creatives. Because of multi-ad sequencing and last-click reporting, ad-level ROAS is the least reliable number in the account; a 6x ad may just be the closer of a sequence. Grouping at the ad set level, for example a 3x across all ads, is much more dependable. Some cross-serving between ad sets still happens: one ad set may show 4x and another 3x partly because the first picks up bottom of funnel purchases started by the second. Keeping one distinct concept per ad set limits this. At the campaign level, as long as attribution is 7-day click and existing customers are excluded, Blue Sense finds the number is very consistent with the P&L. How to apply: make scaling and kill decisions at ad set and campaign level; use ad-level numbers only as rough signals for creative feedback; and keep concepts separated by ad set so the ad set reads are clean.
conditions: Meta accounts using concept-level ad sets and 7-day click reporting.
fails_when: Campaigns still reporting on 1-day view or including existing customers, where even campaign ROAS overstates the P&L.
numbers: example ad set 3x versus ad set 4x with cross-serving

claim: Rank metrics in a pyramid: platform ROAS and CPA at the base (fast, least reliable), finance metrics like acquisition MER and contribution in the middle, lift studies at the top (slow, most reliable); make big decisions from the top two.
body: Blue Sense uses a three level pyramid to decide how much trust a number deserves. The base is attributed numbers: ROAS, CPA, CTR, multi-touch attribution. They update daily and help compare ads and campaigns inside one platform, but they rest on correlation. The middle is finance grade metrics that do not use attribution at all: profit contribution, MER, acquisition MER, CAC, new customer revenue. They come from the store and the P&L, so they are much more reliable, but you need longer windows to read them because daily numbers bounce. The top is lift studies and geo tests with real control and treatment groups, which give causal answers but take weeks and cost money. How to apply: use platform metrics for day to day ad and campaign moves within one platform; use finance metrics for weekly budget levels and channel mix; reserve lift tests for the largest bets (new channels, big budget shifts, TV or outdoor). Never make a business level decision, such as cutting a channel or moving budget between platforms, on base level metrics alone.
conditions: Any brand reporting on paid media; the top layer matters mainly above $5M to $20M revenue or multi-channel spend.
fails_when: Single-channel small stores, where finance metrics and platform metrics nearly agree and lift tests are too costly.

claim: Read revenue from gross to net, not just net: Xero and QuickBooks often show only net, so a month-on-month change may come entirely from refunds, discounts or shipping collected, which are profit levers.
body: Gross revenue is everything collected at the top line. Net revenue subtracts returns, refunds, chargebacks and often a discount allowance. Shopify shows the breakdown, but Blue Sense notes it usually does not flow into accounting tools like Xero or QuickBooks, which record only the net or cash figure. That hides the reason for changes. Example: net revenue goes from $100k to $110k. Looking only at net, you hunt through marketing and staffing for the cause. Looking above net, gross was $120k in both months; refunds fell from $20k to $10k. The growth came from fewer refunds. It could equally be a discount code that ran one month and not the next. These lines are direct levers: cut refunds, cut discounting, or collect more shipping at checkout (Blue Sense says most stores under-collect) and profit rises without more ad spend. How to apply: build a monthly gross to net table from Shopify (gross sales, discounts, returns, shipping charged, net sales) beside the P&L, review it before diagnosing any revenue change, and set targets for refund rate, discount rate and shipping recovered.
conditions: Shopify brands using Xero, QuickBooks or similar accounting tools; especially fashion and other high return categories.
fails_when: Brands whose accounting setup already imports Shopify's gross to net detail.
numbers: example gross $120k both months; refunds $20k versus $10k; net $100k versus $110k

claim: Run geo-lift tests by grouping regions whose spend, new customer revenue and new customer orders moved together, then change spend in one group (for example cut 50% for 30 days) and compare against the other.
body: A geo-lift test is the gold standard once revenue is captured in many places (site, retail, Amazon, wholesale) and spend runs on several channels. Steps Blue Sense describes: 1) Pull daily history by region for ad spend, new customer revenue and new customer orders (orders guard against swings in order value). 2) Use a clustering approach to find regions that track each other; single regions rarely match, so combine them, for example Arizona plus Texas against New York plus California. Combinations also reduce the risk of one odd region. 3) Confirm the control group predicts the treatment group's revenue closely before the test. 4) Make one change in the treatment group: cut spend 50% for 30 days, double a Meta cold campaign, add TikTok, or run outdoor or TV only there. 5) Compare actual results with what the control predicted (the counterfactual). If revenue falls in proportion to the spend cut, ads were fully incremental; if it does not fall, the spend was wasted. Example: an extra $40,000 Meta spend producing $100,000 above the predicted baseline is a 2.5 incremental ROAS. You can also read retail revenue in the same regions to catch offline effects.
conditions: Brands spending tens to hundreds of thousands a month, ideally $20M+ revenue, with enough regions and stable history; someone on the team with data science skills.
fails_when: Small budgets that cannot move regional revenue enough to read; DIY versions in a spreadsheet, which Blue Sense says almost always wrongly show every region as incremental; markets with too few regions.

claim: Set CAC targets from first purchase gross profit of new customers only: blended AOV includes returning buyers' bigger baskets, so a $100 AOV may be $90 for new buyers and margin lower after entry discounts.
body: A CAC figure means nothing without a pairing number, and that number is gross profit on the first purchase. A $100 CAC is excellent if the first order earns $10,000 of gross profit (high ticket furniture), and terrible if it earns $20 (cheap lollies), where each new customer loses $80. The common error is to take Shopify's average order value and a blended margin and conclude, for example, $100 AOV times 70% is $70 of gross profit, so a $35 CAC is fine. Returning customers usually spend more per order, which lifts the blended AOV, and first orders often use discount-led offers, which lowers their margin. Split out new customers and the AOV may be $90 and gross profit $50, so the CAC target built on $70 was wrong. How to apply: in Shopify, filter orders to first-time customers, calculate their average order value and average discount, apply true gross margin from tagged COGS, and set the CAC ceiling as a share of that first-order gross profit (for example half of it for a 2x first-purchase ratio). Recalculate whenever the new customer offer changes.
conditions: Brands with meaningful repeat purchase or discount-led acquisition offers.
fails_when: Brands with no repeat customers and no entry offers, where blended and new customer AOV match.
numbers: example blended $100 AOV at 70% = $70 GP; new customer $90 AOV with $50 GP

claim: Small budgets on Snapchat, Pinterest or Reddit usually report high ROAS because low-spend delivery drifts to warm site visitors in the pixel; they add little new growth until the main channels are maxed out.
body: When a platform gets only a small share of budget, its algorithm finds the cheapest conversions it can, and those are people already in the pixel who recently visited your site. They buy anyway, the channel claims them, and the reported ROAS looks excellent. Blue Sense lists these low-spend tertiary channels as a recurring audit problem: they add management time and confusing numbers while driving almost no new customers. Its broader rule (the profit frontier) is to push each main channel, typically Meta, Google and TikTok, to the point where an extra dollar no longer earns more than break-even acquisition MER, and only then add new channels. How to apply: for each small channel, check the share of spend going to existing or engaged audiences, compare new customer revenue in weeks with and without it, and either fund it properly with a measurable test (geo or holdout) or switch it off and move the budget to the main channel with the best next-dollar return.
conditions: Brands spending small amounts on several extra platforms alongside one or two main ones.
fails_when: Categories where a smaller platform is the main discovery channel (for example Pinterest for some home and wedding products) and is funded at real scale.

claim: Switch Meta reporting from 7-day click, 1-day view to 7-day click, 1-day engaged; in Blue Sense audits 30 to 50% of reported ROAS comes from 1-day view conversions.
body: Meta's default setting counts a sale if someone clicked an ad and bought within 7 days, engaged with it within a day, or simply had the ad appear in their feed and bought within 24 hours. That last part, 1-day view, needs no watching, no click and no interaction. Warm visitors and existing customers who were going to buy anyway see an ad in passing and Meta takes the credit. Blue Sense lists 1-day view running across all campaigns and used in reporting as the number one mistake in its audits, and says removing it typically strips 30 to 50% of reported ROAS. How to apply: for new campaigns, set attribution to 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view. For existing campaigns, change the reporting view: in Ads Manager open Columns, choose Compare attribution settings, and add 7-day click. Make budget and kill decisions on that number. Blue Sense finds 7-day click ROAS tracks acquisition MER in the P&L much more closely than the default view. Keep 1-day engaged because, after Meta's 2026 change, that bucket now holds the likes, comments and profile clicks that used to count as clicks.
conditions: Meta accounts with a meaningful warm or existing customer audience; mature brands where many viewers already know you.
fails_when: Brand new stores with almost no existing customers, where view-through credit is smaller; video awareness campaigns judged on reach rather than sales.

30 to 50% of reported ROAS from view-throughs in audits

claim: Tag COGS on every Shopify product so margin updates in real time; a 20% sitewide sale turns a $100 item with $50 cost into a 37.5% margin, about a 25% relative drop most models miss.
body: LTGP to CAC, profit contribution and break-even targets all need live gross margin. Many brands instead give their agency one average from the accountant, such as 50%, and every model multiplies revenue by it. That breaks during sales. Example: $100 product, $50 cost of delivery, 50% margin. On Black Friday at 20% off, the price drops to $80 but cost stays $50, so gross profit falls to $30 and margin to 37.5%. Bigger baskets raise order value, but margin is set per unit, so the fixed 50% assumption overstates profit exactly when you spend the most. How to apply: in Shopify, fill in the cost per item field on every product and variant (include landed cost, not just the factory price), so Shopify's reports and any connected dashboard or Google Sheet calculate margin on actual selling prices, including discount periods. Then set separate efficiency targets for sale periods instead of using your normal ones. Without tagged COGS you are forced into a single percentage that will mislead budget decisions.
conditions: Shopify stores that run discounts or promotions; any brand computing profit from a blended margin percentage.
fails_when: Brands that never discount and sell one product with stable costs, where a fixed percentage is close enough.

claim: Third party multi-touch tools cannot see the true first touch; Blue Sense often found first clicks credited to brand search, which would wrongly push budget into branded search instead of what created demand.
body: The two interactions that matter most in a buying journey are the first one (how people discover you) and the last one (what closes the sale). Last click is already visible inside each platform, so an extra tool adds little there. First click is the part you would pay a tool for, and it is close to unknowable, because cookies and identity break somewhere along the way. Blue Sense spent hundreds of hours inside these tools and, looking at single buyers' journeys, often saw the first touch listed as a brand search. That cannot be the true start: something made them search the name. In fashion it might be a friend wearing the product. Acting on the tool would mean putting more money into brand search when the real need is more of whatever happened off screen. How to apply: do not use multi-touch first click reports for budget allocation. Use a post-purchase 'how did you hear about us' survey for discovery, and finance metrics plus lift tests to judge channels. Keep last click data inside each platform for within-platform optimisation only.
conditions: Brands considering or already paying for attribution software such as Triple Whale.
fails_when: Closed ecosystems with logged in users across touchpoints, where journeys really can be stitched.

claim: To judge a channel you launched without a test, use Google's open source CausalImpact model to predict what revenue would have done from spend, keyword seasonality and other drivers, then compare with actual.
body: Most channel launches are not set up as experiments. A brand starts YouTube or TikTok in October, has a great November, and credits the new channel, when November is always strong. CausalImpact, an open source package Google released about a decade ago, gives a rough retrospective answer. You load daily new customer revenue and the variables you believe drive it: ad spend on other channels, keyword search seasonality, influencer spend, even inflation data. The model learns how revenue moved with those inputs before the launch and predicts what revenue would have been after it without the change. The gap between predicted and actual is the estimated effect. In Blue Sense's example, YouTube added about $10,000 of revenue for $10,000 of spend, a 1x return, far below what the team assumed. Blue Sense builds this into its internal software to check past launches. How to apply: use it for direction (did the channel do something or nothing), not for exact ROAS, because it is a predictive model on outside variables, not a controlled test. For future launches, plan a geo test instead.
conditions: Brands with at least a year of daily data and a team member comfortable with R or Python.
fails_when: Launches that coincided with big promotions or seasonal peaks the model cannot separate; short data histories.

claim: Tripling a brand in a year usually needs debt; about five times Blue Sense saw agencies lift spend from $20k to $200k a month and revenue from $2M to $7M while net profit fell near zero.
body: Fast growth in ecommerce needs cash for future stock, so a brand growing quickly must have big personal funds, investors, or inventory finance. Blue Sense describes seeing, about five times, an agency take a seven-figure client from $20,000 to $200,000 a month in ad spend with no visibility into the client's finances. Behind the scenes the founder borrowed millions in inventory finance to buy stock for that growth. As spend rose, marketing efficiency fell, and interest payments grew, until net margin was squeezed to around zero. Revenue went from about $2M to $7M a year, but a business that had been cash positive and paying the founder now made almost nothing after interest. The trap is lowering efficiency to grow faster, which also increases the debt needed. Blue Sense's view: grow a little slower at a better MER, with less marketing spend and less interest, and make far more money. How to apply: before agreeing a growth plan, model revenue, MER, inventory purchases, financing and interest month by month, and compare net profit and cash across two or three growth rates.
conditions: Seven and low eight figure brands using or considering inventory finance to fund rapid growth.
fails_when: Well-capitalised brands where investors accept low profit for share, or products with short cash cycles.

claim: Turn geo-lift results into incrementality factors and multiply each channel and campaign type's reported ROAS by them, so daily platform numbers reflect real incremental return.
body: A single lift test answers one question once. Larger brands get ongoing value by converting results into multipliers. As an illustration (these figures are ours, not the video's), if a geo test shows a Meta prospecting campaign reported 4x but drove 2x incrementally, its factor is 0.5; if DPAs reported 8x but drove 1.6x, their factor is 0.2. Apply these to the in-platform ROAS in your dashboard so the daily numbers the team reacts to are adjusted for what each campaign type really adds. That keeps the speed of platform data while borrowing the reliability of the tests. The catch is that factors go stale as creative, spend levels and channel mix change, so Blue Sense says you need to run geo tests often and across every major channel and campaign type to keep factors current. How to apply: keep a table of factors by platform and campaign type with the test date, apply them in your BI layer or sheet, and schedule re-tests, prioritising the largest spend lines first.
conditions: Brands of roughly $20M+ revenue running regular geo or lift tests across several channels.
fails_when: Brands that have run only one test; a single old factor applied for months can be more misleading than none.

claim: Two campaigns at the same 4x ROAS can return very different profit, because discount codes, product margin and new versus returning mix change the margin behind each dollar of revenue.
body: ROAS treats every dollar of attributed revenue as equal. It is not. One campaign may sell full price retention orders, another may lean on an entry discount code or push lower margin products. Both can show $10,000 of attributed revenue at 4x, yet one might return the equivalent of 3x in profit contribution and the other 4x. On ROAS alone they look tied; on contribution the second clearly deserves more budget. How to apply: for each major campaign, estimate the gross margin of what it actually sells (product mix and average discount used), subtract ad spend and cost of delivery, and rank campaigns by contribution profit, not ROAS. Pull the products sold per campaign from Shopify or your attribution export, and apply real margins from COGS tagged on each product. This is also why one blended target ROAS across the account misleads you: a promo campaign and a full price campaign need different targets to make the same profit.
conditions: Accounts with several campaigns selling different product groups, promo versus full price, or new versus returning buyers.
fails_when: Single product stores with one price and no discounting, where margin per order is the same in every campaign.
numbers: example: two campaigns each at 4x ROAS on $10,000 attributed revenue; profit view 3 versus 4

claim: Use a short LTGP to CAC window (30 or 90 days) to track yourself, and extend to 180 or 365 days when comparing with other brands or categories, because repeat cycles differ.
body: Lifetime value keeps rising the longer you measure it, so an uncapped LTV makes any CAC look affordable and leads to overspending on cash you will not see back for years. Blue Sense always caps the window. For tracking your own brand over time, any fixed window works: 30, 90 or 180 days, as long as it stays the same. Blue Sense typically tracks 30-day and 90-day, and adds 365-day when the acquisition strategy is aggressive. When comparing against other businesses, especially in other categories, lengthen the window. A CPG brand may run a low first purchase gross profit to CAC but make far more over a year because of high repeat rates, while a fashion brand earns more up front and repeats less. Comparing them on 30 days would rank them wrongly. How to apply: build cohorts by first order month in Shopify or your analytics tool, sum gross profit per cohort at 30, 90 and 180 days (using cost of delivery, not revenue), and divide by that month's CAC. Report your own trend on one window and compare to peers on the longer one.
conditions: Brands with at least several months of cohort history and repeat purchasing.
fails_when: One-time purchase categories (furniture, big ticket items) where only first order gross profit matters.

claim: When a P&L line misses target, the cause sits in the lines above it: a missed EBITDA points to opex, marketing or cost of delivery; a missed gross margin points to delivery costs, refunds or discounts.
body: Blue Sense reads the P&L as a waterfall with a target percentage at each level, tracked month on month. Example shape: cost of delivery 40%, gross margin 60%, marketing (MER) 20%, contribution 40%, opex 20%, EBITDA 20%, net profit 10% after interest. Because each level is the result of everything above it, a miss can only be explained upward. If EBITDA is off target, look at opex, marketing and cost of delivery. If contribution is off, look at marketing efficiency and cost of delivery. If gross margin is off, look at cost of delivery and at the revenue lines above net: discounting, returns and refunds, shipping collected. If MER is creeping up, marketing efficiency is falling and squeezing everything below. How to apply: put the percentage for each level in a monthly table with the target beside it, flag any level outside target, and only investigate the lines above the first one that missed. This keeps a team from, for example, cutting ad spend to fix a margin problem that was really caused by a discount campaign or a jump in returns.
conditions: Brands with a monthly P&L in a consistent structure (cost of delivery, marketing, opex separated).
fails_when: P&Ls where costs are misclassified, for example fulfilment staff in opex, which sends the diagnosis to the wrong line.
numbers: example waterfall: COD 40%, GM 60%, MER 20%, CM 40%, opex 20%, EBITDA 20%, net 10%
