claim: When unsold November stock is still sitting in February, cutting media 40% can start a spiral; Blue Sense would instead raise MER briefly, for example from 30% to 35%, to turn grade C and D stock into cash.
body: A common Q1 conflict: inventory bought for November has not sold, cash is tight, revenue dips, and MER jumps (in Blue Sense's example from 25% to 30% of revenue) while profit falls from 30% to 25%. The CFO's reflex is to cut marketing by 40%. Two problems. If marketing really drives revenue, cutting it lowers revenue further, which pushes MER up again, which leads to more cuts, a loop that never fixes profit. And the stuck stock still needs to sell to free cash. Blue Sense's counter-intuitive answer is to spend more for a short period: deliberately accept MER of about 35%, with the extra 5% dedicated to clearing grade C and D stock, accepting it is not profitable spend, so inventory turns back into cash and the business can return to its normal revenue position. How to apply: when cash is tight, separate the efficiency problem on core spend from the stock problem. Fix efficiency on core campaigns with creative and offer work; run a time-limited, separately budgeted clearance push with its own cash recovery goal; and agree both with finance before cutting anything.
conditions: Brands where paid media drives most new revenue and excess seasonal stock exists.
fails_when: Brands where marketing is not the main revenue driver, or where the stock cannot sell even at break-even.

claim: Check spend on existing customers first: Nathan finds overspend on them in about 90% of accounts, from missing exclusions or 7-day click 1-day view settings that favour view-through buyers.
body: Nathan's first question in any e-commerce account is how much spend reaches existing customers compared with new ones. He estimates about 90% of accounts overspend on existing customers. Two causes: existing customers are not excluded where they could be, or the account optimises on 7-day click 1-day view, which gives credit to people who saw an ad and later bought, and those are mostly people already on the site or in the customer list. Caden agreed that almost every account they take over leans too heavily on warm traffic, which shows up quickly when you compare server side data with spend. Both like the fix of building a new customer purchase event, a purchase from someone buying for the first time, sent back into the ad platform as the event to optimise for, with first click credit. Other Blue Sense cards cover judging on acquisition MER; what this adds is the scale of the problem and the event based fix. How to check: in Shopify, compare new customer orders with ad spend by month; in Meta, read the audience segment breakdown where it is available; in Google, look at the new customer acquisition goal and customer lists. If new customers are flat while spend rises, exclude buyers where possible, move reporting off 1-day view, and set up the new customer event.
conditions: E-commerce brands with a real repeat customer base and enough new customer purchases to optimise on.
fails_when: New stores with few past customers; subscription or replenishment brands that plan retention spend on purpose; the 90% figure is an estimate from accounts he reviews.

claim: Across about $150M of Meta spend, Blue Sense sees CPMs rise roughly 20% to 30% a year, so plans must assume conversion rate or order value gains just to hold CPA.
body: Meta grows revenue in two ways: more ad slots in the feed, and higher prices per thousand impressions once the feed is full. Blue Sense ran an aggregated report across the roughly $150M in spend linked to its business manager and saw CPMs climb about 20% to 30% each year, cycling around Black Friday but rising year on year, faster than general inflation. Meta cannot price everyone out, so it also works to raise expected conversion rates, which is what each delivery update aims at. How to apply in planning: when you build next year's paid budget, do not copy this year's CPM. Lift it by 20% to 30% and check what conversion rate, order value or margin you need to keep cost per new customer flat. If the model only works at today's CPM, plan the site, offer and creative work that will close the gap, rather than hoping costs stay put.

fails_when: A brand's own CPMs are moving for other reasons (new markets, new placements, a big creative change), or a short window like Q1 shows seasonal drops that hide the yearly trend.

claim: A flat CAC can hide trouble: first-order gross profit at one brand swung from about $40 in November to $70 in August because of product mix and discount margin, so track both sides monthly.
body: Many brands audited by Blue Sense watch CAC closely and keep it flat, say $50 every month, and assume the business is steady. They do not track the other side of the ratio. When Blue Sense looks at gross profit on the first purchase, it moves a lot: around $40 in November, so the brand loses money on each new customer, and around $70 in August. The swings come from product mix shifting toward lower-margin items and from margin compression during discount events. The cohorts differ too: November cohorts repeat worse than others, so the gap widens as you extend the LTGP window. How to apply: compute first-order gross profit per new customer each month (new-customer revenue minus product, delivery and payment costs, after refunds) next to CAC, and flag any month where the ratio drops under your target even if CAC held. Plan sale months with a lower CAC ceiling, because their customers are worth less on day one and often later.
conditions: Brands with seasonal discounting or a product range with very different margins.
fails_when: Single-product brands with stable pricing and no promotions, where first-order gross profit barely moves.

claim: Calculate CAC and LTGP every month, log the date of every big change (new agency, platform such as Snapchat, product launch), and repeat only changes that improved the ratio.
body: Blue Sense's action plan is simple. Each month, compute CAC and LTGP. Low-retention businesses such as furniture and homewares can use first-purchase gross profit; fashion and CPG should use a 180-day window from a real cohort analysis, never a made-up number. If CAC is rising or LTGP falling, troubleshoot that specific metric. Then keep a dated log of structural changes: a new creative agency, a big jump in ad volume, adding a platform like Snapchat, a new product launch aimed at LTGP. Check each change against the two core numbers. Their example: a product launched in March lifted LTGP, as expected because a wider range creates cross-sell; if you can repeat that without putting the balance sheet at risk, do it again. The reason this matters: a healthy-looking total P&L can mask decay. One client looked fine at $80,000 to $100,000 monthly profit, but its first-time customer P&L had gone from about $20,000 profit to about $70,000 loss a month, hidden by repeat purchases. How to apply: add a change log tab to your monthly KPI sheet next to the two metrics.
conditions: Any brand with paid acquisition and enough history to compare months.

claim: First-order losses can be funded only by repeat-customer profit, investors or debt; split the P&L by Shopify order type to see it, for example $50,000 a month lost on new buyers against $300,000 returning profit.
body: If you lose money on first purchases, something has to pay for it. Blue Sense lists three sources. First, repeat-customer profit: they split a client's P&L into a first-time customer P&L and a returning customer P&L by filtering every line on Shopify's order type tag. A brand might lose $50,000 a month on first-time customers yet make $300,000 on returning ones, so the business is profitable while acquisition loses money. Second, investors: raising capital can be the right call, and many fast-scaling brands have used it. Third, creditors or debt. Blue Sense's caution is that the last two need an advanced operator, ideally someone who has built an eight-figure business before, because debt makes profitability harder to see; they say they would not take on a $6 to $7 million brand with investors or creditors because of the risk. How to apply: build the split P&L (or simply track LTGP to CAC, which tells the same story at unit level), and only accept first-order losses that the returning P&L clearly covers.

claim: Measure retention only through cohort analysis on gross profit, not Klaviyo attributed revenue, daily returning revenue or Shopify's new customer share; read 90-day LTGP to CAC per cohort month.
body: Most brands do not know whether retention is improving, so they cannot tell if LTGP to CAC is getting better. Blue Sense rules out the usual proxies: Klaviyo attributed revenue, returning-customer revenue by day or month, and the share of new customers in Shopify. The only method they trust is a cohort table: each row is the customers acquired in a month, month zero shows what they spent at first, and the following columns show cumulative value at day 30, 60, 90 and so on. Shopify has a cohort report but shows revenue, not gross profit, so Blue Sense builds its own with actual product costs; applying an assumed margin percentage to Shopify's revenue cohort is a fallback, not the ideal. To get a 90-day LTGP to CAC, take the 90-day cumulative gross profit per customer for a cohort month and divide by that same month's CAC. How to apply: build the gross profit cohort monthly, plot the 90-day ratio by cohort, and judge retention projects by whether new cohorts beat older ones at the same age.
conditions: Brands with at least several months of order history and access to product cost data.

claim: Most DTC failures trace to one ratio, LTGP to CAC: average first-order contribution fell from $9 in 2013 to a $29 loss in 2022, and Casper still lost $300 per mattress after $423M of ads.
body: Blue Sense opens with a 2022 industry report: in 2013 the average ecommerce brand made $9 contribution margin on a first-time customer; by 2022 it lost $29. Their examples of where this ends: SmileDirectClub listed at an $8.9 billion valuation and was liquidated four years later, and Casper spent over $423 million on advertising in four years while still losing about $300 per mattress. None of these brands thought they had a structural problem; they blamed creative, the ad account or growth. Blue Sense says the failures collapse into the same equation: lifetime gross profit (after product and delivery costs) over a fixed window, divided by CAC (total ad spend divided by new customers). If that ratio is bad, more capital or more spend will not save the business. How to apply: before diagnosing creative or media, compute 30-day LTGP to CAC by month for the last 12 to 24 months; if it is trending down, the fix is structural (offer, margin, product, retention), not tactical.
conditions: DTC brands that rely on paid acquisition for growth.
fails_when: Brands whose problem is cash or operating cost rather than unit economics (see the operating expense trap), or wholesale-led brands where ad CAC is a small part of acquisition.

claim: On a 30-day LTGP to CAC ratio, under 1 loses money, 1 to 2 rarely clears 20% net unless opex is very lean, 2 to 3 is where to scale, and above 3 means under-spending.
body: Ecommerce differs from agencies and software, which often break even only in month four to six: consumers are far less sticky than business clients, a second order is lucky and a third or fourth rare, so a store should aim to be profitable and liquid on the first purchase. Blue Sense's bands, using 30-day LTGP (close to first-order gross profit): under 1, for example $100 gross profit against $120 CAC (0.83), loses $20 per new customer, and only very strong retention justifies it, which they say almost nobody has. Between 1 and 2, each $1 in ads returns about $1.50 in gross profit, leaving only 50 cents for all operating costs; a very lean operator with good retention might reach about 20% net, but most will not. 2 to 3 is the zone where they push budgets. Above 3 there is no reason to hold back; you are leaving profitable volume unbought. How to apply: compute the ratio monthly and treat it as the go or no-go signal for scaling spend, with the band boundaries as triggers.

fails_when: Subscription or high-repeat CPG brands with proven cohort paybacks, which can run below 1 on 30 days if longer-window LTGP covers it and cash allows.

claim: Platform ROAS can hide decline: one large Australian retailer showed a steady 20 ROAS in Meta that fell to 7 without view-through conversions and to 4 on incremental attribution, and that figure was falling.
body: At eight and nine figures, the most common way CAC slips unnoticed for months is that the team watches in-platform ROAS. Blue Sense describes a well-known Australian retailer: Meta and Google reported a ROAS of about 20, flat for a year, while profit was sinking. Removing view-through conversions dropped Meta ROAS to about 7, and moving to incremental attribution dropped it to about 4. The 4 had been declining over time; the 20 was not connected to what was actually happening. Their principle: the best decisions come from metrics as close as possible to base reality, and attributed numbers sit further away. You can still use attribution, but check that the version you use moves with real CAC. How to apply: in Ads Manager compare click-only attribution with your default; add an incrementality read (a lift test, a holdout or an incremental attribution setting); and plot each against blended new-customer CAC monthly. Make decisions on the version that tracks CAC, and treat a flat platform ROAS during rising CAC as a warning, not comfort.
conditions: Brands spending heavily on Meta and Google, where view-through and overlapping credit inflate platform ROAS.
fails_when: Small accounts with mostly click-based conversions and little channel overlap, where platform ROAS and blended numbers move together.

claim: Rank measurement by closeness to reality: opinion, then platform ROAS (simple correlation), then marketing mix models, then quasi-experiments, then a geo holdout; LTGP to CAC is the business-level truth.
body: Blue Sense lays out an evidence ladder for judging marketing. At the bottom is expert opinion and anecdote. Next is simple correlation, which is what platform ROAS and attribution are. Above that is advanced correlation that adjusts for outside factors through multiple regression, such as marketing mix models. Then come quasi-experiments, for example a difference-in-differences design or a regression discontinuity, better than MMMs or ROAS but still imperfect. At the top is a true experiment: a geo holdout, where you switch a channel off in some regions and compare. The higher you go, the closer you are to what really happened. For the business as a whole, LTGP to CAC is the final scorecard; the ladder is how you work out which of several platforms is helping or hurting that ratio. How to apply: when channels disagree, do not argue over attributed numbers; pick the highest rung you can afford for the channel in question (often a geo holdout for a big spend line) and use the result to re-weight budgets.
conditions: Brands spending across several paid platforms who need to know which ones drive new customers.
fails_when: Spend is too small or concentrated in one market to run a geo holdout with readable results; quasi-experiments or careful on-off tests are then the practical top rung.

claim: The death spiral: CAC creeps from $50 to $60, a fixed budget buys fewer customers, revenue drops, spend is raised to compensate, CAC rises again; Blue Sense saw it in about 100 of 1,000+ audits.
body: The loop works like this. CAC drifts up, say from $50 to $60. With a stable budget (for example $100,000) you buy fewer new customers, so revenue falls. If repeat purchasing is weak, nothing props revenue up, so the team raises spend to hold the top line. Spending more pushes into colder audiences and CAC climbs again, and may lower LTGP too. Within months the brand spends far more for a CAC twice the old level. Blue Sense says it has seen this in roughly 100 cases among over 1,000 brands audited, visible in month-by-month CAC against new customer volume: at some point CAC jumps, spend is cranked up, and CAC never recovers. Brands usually arrive about four months in, convinced the cause is traffic, creative or seasonality. It usually is not. How to apply: chart monthly CAC, new customers, spend and 30-day LTGP together. If CAC rises while you raise spend to hold revenue, stop scaling, find which input moved (CPM, click rate, conversion rate, first-order gross profit) and fix that before adding budget.
conditions: Brands that rely on paid media for most new customers and have weak repeat revenue.
fails_when: Brands with strong repeat revenue that cushions a CAC rise, or where CAC rose for a known one-off reason (for example a short seasonal auction spike).

claim: Your achievable LTGP is set mainly by category: fashion lifts about 55% by day 365, CPG about 110%, most brands only 20% to 40%, and furniture near zero, so set CAC to match.
body: Blue Sense estimates that about 80% of brands watching have little meaningful lifetime gross profit: customers buy, some return, and by day 365 gross profit per customer is maybe 20%, 30% or 40% above the first order. Benchmarks they give for retention-friendly categories: fashion about 55% lift by day 365, consumables (CPG) about 110%. Some categories have almost none. Furniture is bought when people move house, it is expensive, and the next purchase may be three to five years away, so for B2C furniture clients they ignore LTGP and manage first-purchase gross profit against a CAC that must stay flat. Retention tactics help at the edges, but the band you can reach is largely built into the category; a $50 keratin supplement will never support a huge LTGP. How to apply: look at where the best brands in your category sit, set your own LTGP expectation near but below them, and build CAC targets on that realistic number. Low-retention businesses should simply track first-purchase gross profit each month; higher-retention ones should use a 180-day window from real cohorts.

Without the store's own numbers you cannot tell whether a rising ROAS is real or whether cost to acquire a customer has quietly doubled. claim: Build a monthly table going back 2 to 2.5 years of CAC (total ad spend divided by new customers) beside dollar gross profit on the first purchase, because CAC alone misleads when AOV and margin have moved.
body: This is the first sheet in a Blue Sense audit. Column one is the month, going back about two to two and a half years. Column two is CAC: all advertising spend that month divided by new customers acquired that month. On its own CAC is misleading, because a brand that once sold a $100 order at 60% gross profit and now sells a $200 order at 80% can afford a much higher CAC today. So column three is gross profit in dollars on the first order. Two ways to get it: multiply each month's average order value by that month's gross margin percentage from an accrual-basis P&L, or, if cost of goods has been loaded into Shopify historically, pull the average gross profit on first orders report directly. Use the real margin for each month, not one flat assumption across the whole period, or the trend you are trying to read disappears. Add a new customer count column too, since you already need it for CAC. The next step divides gross profit by CAC.
conditions: Brands with at least a year of paid history and either an accrual P&L or cost of goods recorded in Shopify.
fails_when: Subscription or very high repeat brands where the first order is deliberately a loss leader; first-order maths then needs a retention adjustment before it can guide spend.
numbers: look back 2 to 2.5 years by month
example: $100 AOV at 60% GP then, $200 AOV at 80% GP now
CAC = total ad spend / new customers per month

claim: Build a second P&L using first-time orders only, because accumulated repeat revenue can make paid acquisition look healthy when it is not; it also gives acquisition MER (new customer revenue divided by ad spend).
body: Large retailers with years of repeat buyers can show a strong overall P&L while their paid acquisition loses money, because returning customers prop up the totals. To see acquisition clearly, rebuild the same P&L with every returning customer order filtered out, so only first orders remain. All the same lines apply: net revenue, cost of goods, fulfilment, fees, marketing and contribution margin, but on new customers alone. This view also hands you acquisition MER: revenue from new customers divided by total ad spend. That number is the yardstick for the next audit step, where each platform's reported ROAS is compared with it. How to apply: in Shopify, filter orders by customer type for first-time purchases, export by month, and run the P&L lines on that subset. If the first-time P&L shows negative contribution while the blended one looks fine, treat paid as the problem regardless of what the ad platforms report.
conditions: Brands with meaningful repeat purchase revenue, especially eight figures and up; needs new versus returning order tagging.
fails_when: Very young brands with almost no repeat revenue, where both P&Ls look the same and the extra work adds nothing.
numbers: acquisition MER = new customer revenue / ad spend

claim: First-purchase gross profit divided by CAC reads: under 1 is losing money, 1 to 2 is only okay, 2 to 3 is where you should scale, and above 3 means you are underspending.
body: Divide each month's dollar gross profit on the first order by that month's CAC. Blue Sense calls the result GP to CAC on first purchase and treats it as the best single index of acquisition efficiency over time. Their rough bands: below 1, every new customer costs more than the profit their first order makes; unless you are a sophisticated CPG brand with strong repeat buying or are raising capital, this is a bankruptcy risk. Between 1 and 2 is acceptable but they would not push spend in most businesses unless retention is very good. Between 2 and 3 is the target zone where you should be scaling. Above 3 you are leaving growth on the table and should spend more, unless another acquisition channel outside this sum is doing the work. Chart the ratio by month: a falling line over the last six months is where the audit starts digging. Adjust the bands for retention: strong 90, 180 and 365-day gross profit growth lets you accept a lower first-order ratio, weak retention means you need the higher end.
conditions: DTC brands where most revenue comes from paid acquisition and first-order margin is known; bands are generalisations across Blue Sense's portfolio.
fails_when: Strong subscription or replenishment brands where lifetime gross profit dwarfs the first order, or brands with large unpaid channels (organic, retail) feeding new customers that the CAC sum ignores.

claim: If acquisition MER is 3x to 7x but Meta reports ROAS near 17, the gap is usually spend on existing customers or 1-day view; compare 7-day click, 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view and incremental attribution columns.
body: Blue Sense's worked example: a large retailer spending $100,000 a month whose first-time P&L shows $300,000 to $700,000 in new customer revenue, so acquisition MER of 3x to 7x. Meta's account-wide ROAS says 17. The usual causes are budget leaking onto existing customers, which inflates platform ROAS, or 1-day view attribution claiming people who saw an ad but were going to buy anyway. How to check: in Ads Manager open Columns, then compare attribution settings, and look at 7-day click, 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view, and Meta's incremental attribution. In about 95% of accounts they see these line up much more closely with acquisition MER. You then have two choices: switch the optimisation setting to whichever window tracks the business best, or keep running as is but always judge performance on that tighter column. Either way, stop moving budget on a ROAS number that has no link to new customer revenue, because every daily decision built on it compounds the error.
conditions: Meta accounts where the business can compute acquisition MER monthly; the 3x to 7x range describes large retailers.
fails_when: Brands with long consideration cycles or heavy offline sales, where view-through may capture real influence; very small accounts where monthly MER is too noisy to compare.

claim: Lay out a normalised P&L for the same 2.5 years down to contribution margin (gross revenue less refunds and discounts plus shipping, less COGS, fulfilment and fees, less marketing) and check it does not fall while spend rises.
body: The unit view (CAC and gross profit per customer) is checked against a volume view. Build a normalised monthly P&L. Revenue block: gross revenue, minus refunds and returns, minus discounts, plus shipping collected, gives net revenue. Then subtract cost of goods, shipping and fulfilment, and payment transaction fees to reach gross margin. Subtract all marketing (you can split Meta, Google and influencer, or keep one line) to reach contribution margin, which is contribution margin 3 if you name the layers. An in-house team can continue to operating expenses and EBITDA, but an agency auditing a client does not need opex. The key read: if ad spend has been ramped up to scale but contribution margin dollars or percentage went down, the scaling plan rested on a wrong assumption. Find the month the push started and work out which assumption failed, such as expecting new revenue at higher spend that never came, before spending more.
conditions: Brands with monthly accrual accounts or a reliable Shopify plus accounting export.
fails_when: Cash-basis books where costs land in the wrong month, which makes monthly contribution margin swing for reasons unrelated to ads.

On Pinterest, add the 7-day click ROAS column and Blue Sense expects it to line up quickly with business numbers, and often show the channel well below the account average. On TikTok, 1-day view does most of the inflating; cutting to 7-day click usually drops ROAS to acquisition MER and often lower. These channels are typically around 10% of spend in the accounts they audit, so they are checked last, but the habit matters: never fund a channel on a view-through number that you cannot match to new customer revenue. If a channel still looks better than the business after the click-only view, that is the case for a holdout or geo test rather than more budget.

claim: Rising CAC is only a problem if new customer volume is flat; if CAC creeps up while new customers triple or quadruple, the trade can be worth it.
body: After building the monthly table, chart three lines together: new customer volume, CAC and first-order gross profit. Then read them as a set. If CAC has climbed sharply over, say, the last six months and new customer volume has barely moved, total spend must have risen and you are simply paying more for the same customers. That makes CAC the bottleneck and the audit drills into which platform and which campaigns caused it. If CAC has risen a little but new customer volume has grown three or four times, you have traded some efficiency for scale, which is often the right call as long as GP to CAC stays in a healthy band. The outcome of this view is one of three decisions: room to ramp up spend, hold flat and fix things, or pull back fast because you are buying unprofitable cohorts that will hurt cash in three to six months. Check the same story on a normalised P&L before acting, since total volume can tell a slightly different story than unit numbers.
conditions: Brands with steady monthly data and a clear split of new versus returning customers.
fails_when: Seasonal swings (Black Friday, launches) distort single months; compare like-for-like periods before calling a trend.

claim: Set CAC targets with retention in view: Blue Sense benchmarks gross profit growth per cohort at day 90, 180 and 365, and strong retention allows a lower first-purchase GP to CAC.
body: The first-order ratio is only part of the picture. Blue Sense always builds a cohort analysis in gross profit dollars over time and measures how much each cohort's gross profit grows by day 90, day 180 and day 365. They compare that against averages across their client portfolio by category (for example, are you retaining better or worse than their fashion brands, is your 90-day strong but your 365-day weak). The result feeds back into the CAC target. If cohorts grow gross profit strongly, you can tolerate a higher CAC and a first-purchase GP to CAC below the usual 2 to 3 band, because later orders pay back the gap. If retention is poor, which they see often, customers rarely buy twice, so the first order must be clearly profitable on its own. How to apply: from Shopify, group customers by first-order month, sum gross profit per cohort at 90, 180 and 365 days, and express growth as a percentage of first-order gross profit.
conditions: Brands with at least a year of customer history and cost of goods data to compute gross profit per cohort.
fails_when: Brands under a year old, where the 365-day point does not exist yet; the portfolio benchmarks themselves were not shared in the video.

claim: When platform ROAS and business numbers still disagree after changing attribution views, eight and nine figure brands should run a causal geo-lift test of about 25 days, including an inverse test that switches brand search off in clustered states.
body: The cohort model says whether you can scale, hold or must pull back; the P&L confirms it; the correlation check shows whether each platform can be trusted. If after switching attribution columns it is still unclear whether Meta, Google or TikTok drives what it claims, Blue Sense proposes a test rather than a guess. For large brands that is a causal geo-lift experiment: pick test and control regions, change spend in the test regions, and read the difference in business revenue over typically about 25 days. For big retailers convinced their brand search campaigns are incremental, they run it in reverse: turn brand search off in a set of states chosen with a clustering algorithm so they match the rest, and see whether total sales in those states drop. If they do not, the brand budget is mostly paying for customers who would have arrived anyway. Use the result to set spend, not just to report.

claim: A large omnichannel brand's 10x Meta ROAS mostly reflects demand made by search, creators, collabs, stores and events, which Meta then claims at last click; a small brand at 4x is not losing on creative.

Those brands spend heavily on search, creators, brand collaborations, retail stores and events, and Meta records the sale when a buyer who was already won over clicks or views an ad at the end. Blue Sense points to Skims and Nike, whose 2019 drop reportedly took about $2 million in the first few minutes on the back of the collaboration and a waitlist (about half a million people for a 2021 restock); Stanley, which grew from $73 million to $94 million, $194 million and $402 million and roughly doubled after a viral car fire moment; and Gymshark, built on ambassadors and community. Their Meta ads would look superb in Ads Manager while having little to do with the growth. How to apply: when comparing your ROAS to a leader's, first list where their demand comes from. If they have big search, retail, creator or PR engines, discount their Meta results and do not copy their low-funnel aspirational ads. A brand that sells end to end on Meta needs ads that convert strangers, and its in-platform ROAS will look lower.

claim: Consumable and subscription brands can run Meta at about 0.7x to 1x first-order ROAS and stay profitable, because a 3 to 4 month CAC payback lets them push spend into diminishing returns.
body: Smooch (consumable beauty), Hostage Tape (tape that runs out) and Resilia (supplements on subscription) share a model: buyers come back. That raises the most a brand can pay to acquire a customer. Blue Sense estimates these brands can run at roughly 1x or even 0.7x return on the first order, recover acquisition cost in three to four months as repeat orders arrive, break even and then earn on each customer after 6 to 12 months. A brand with one-off purchases has to stop spending when the first order stops being profitable, but these brands can keep spending well past that point, which is how they outscale competitors. How to apply: compute gross profit per customer by month since first order from Shopify cohort data (revenue minus product, shipping, fees and discounts). Find the month where cumulative gross profit passes your cost per new customer; that is your payback. Set your first-order target from what you can fund: if payback is 3 months and cash allows, you can accept a first-order ROAS below break even. Push subscriptions and multi-packs to make repeat orders more certain.

claim: From eight figures a year, run geo holdouts: pick test regions with a clustering method, cut or raise spend there, analyse with Meta's open source GeoLift rather than a spreadsheet, and change budgets on the result.
body: A geo holdout is the most direct read on whether a channel adds sales: change spend in some regions and compare their back-end revenue with matched regions where nothing changed. Blue Sense runs them continuously for large retailers to keep a live read on whether to spend more or less on Meta, TikTok, Google and out of home. How to apply: 1. Choose regions (states in the US or AU) with a clustering algorithm so test and control areas behaved alike before the test, rather than picking by hand. 2. Either turn spend off in the test regions or raise it there, and leave the rest of the country as is. 3. Measure total revenue from Shopify by region, not platform-reported sales. 4. Analyse with a proper package such as Meta's GeoLift; a Google Sheet comparison is highly inaccurate. 5. Most important, act on it: move budget toward the channels that showed lift and away from the ones that did not, and repeat so the mix keeps adjusting. Running a test and then ignoring it is wasted spend.

How to apply: each week, chart new customer revenue, total ad spend and their ratio. As you raise Meta spend, watch whether acquisition MER holds or falls in a straight line with platform ROAS. Then tighten what you report: remove 1-day view from the attribution columns you use for decisions (keep click-based windows), at least in your reporting view. The goal is a platform number that tracks the P&L closely. Once Meta ROAS and acquisition MER rise and fall together, you can trust the daily platform number for optimising; if Meta ROAS climbs while acquisition MER is flat, Meta is claiming sales from other channels or returning customers. This is the first of four checks Blue Sense runs to see whether Meta creates or only harvests demand, alongside brand search response and geo holdouts.

claim: When Meta is creating demand, branded search volume rises as Meta spend rises; Google takes the credit, so read brand search against Meta spend before cutting Meta.
body: Prospecting on Meta puts the brand in front of people who often do not buy on the spot. Some of them search the brand name on Google later and buy there, so the sale is credited to Google brand search, not Meta. If you judge each channel by its own reported return you will over-value brand search and under-value Meta. How to apply: put weekly Meta spend next to weekly branded search impressions and clicks (Google Ads search terms or Search Console queries containing the brand name). Look for brand search lifting a week or two after Meta budget increases and falling after cuts. If brand search tracks Meta spend, count part of brand search revenue as Meta's effect when deciding budgets. If brand search stays flat while Meta spend grows, Meta is probably not adding much new demand. This is the third of the four Blue Sense checks for whether Meta creates or harvests demand.
conditions: Brands running both Meta prospecting and Google brand search with enough volume to see weekly trends.
fails_when: Brands with heavy PR, influencer or TV activity in the same weeks, which also move brand search and blur the link; or tiny brands with too few branded searches to read.

claim: Before a sale, short click windows hide most of the value: Blue Sense sees the 1-day versus 30-day click gap near 40% all year, above 80% in early November, and near zero on Black Friday.
body: A big sale pulls everyone who already knows the brand through to a purchase at the same moment. Shoppers who click an ad in early November often wait for the sale to open and buy then, so a 1-day or 7-day click report gives that spend almost no credit at the time, and later hands the Black Friday weekend credit for sales the earlier spend set up. Blue Sense tracks this as the difference between what 1-day click and 30-day click attribution report. Across a normal year the gap is about 40%. In early November it widens past 80%, because buyers are holding off. On Black Friday it shrinks to almost nothing, because people buy on the day they click. HexClad, a large US cookware brand, showed the size of the effect when it re-credited sale revenue back to the original clicks: spend on 12 and 13 November that read as roughly a 1 ROAS in real time came out near a 4 once 30-day click value had finished booking through the sale. How to apply: in Ads Manager, pull last year's October to December results with 1-day, 7-day and 30-day click columns side by side, note the gap week by week, and use it as a multiplier on real-time pre-sale ROAS instead of cutting spend that only looks weak.
conditions: Brands that run a large, known yearly sale such as Black Friday or Cyber Monday and have last year's Meta data by attribution window; the multiplier must be measured per account.
fails_when: Brands that do not discount or whose buyers do not wait for a sale; small accounts where 30-day click numbers are too noisy; the HexClad figure is one brand's backdated read, not a rule.

gap above 80% in early November
gap close to zero on Black Friday
HexClad: about 1 ROAS in real time on 12 to 13 November became about 4 once value booked (a 300% lift)

claim: Check your November cohorts before setting a BFCM CAC: across 10 Blue Sense clients, November buyers showed a 38.5% six-month repeat lift against 63% for February buyers.
body: Sale buyers are often deal hunters who return less. Blue Sense averaged cohort data across 10 clients by hand: the November cohort delivered a 38.5% repeat lift over six months, the February cohort 63%, close to double. Two of the ten showed no difference at all, so treat this as a check to run, not a rule. How to apply: in Shopify or your retention tool, build cohorts by first order month for the last two years and compare six-month repeat revenue, or gross profit per customer, for November against an ordinary month such as February. If November is clearly worse, set a separate, lower November CAC allowance, because your annual LTV figure overstates what those buyers are worth. Together with the discount, your normal CAC allowance can be wrong twice: once because the first order earns less gross profit, and again because those customers repeat less. If you find no gap, keep your usual LTV-based tolerance.
conditions: Brands with one to two years of cohort data and real repeat purchase behaviour; the sample is 10 Blue Sense clients.
fails_when: One-off purchase categories; brands whose November buyers are mostly buying gifts for others; 2 of the 10 sampled brands showed no gap.

February cohort 63% six-month repeat lift

claim: During BFCM, read Meta on 7-day click (or 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view) and compare several settings, because default attribution overstates and each step down the ladder sits closer to P&L truth.
body: Blue Sense showed an attribution ladder from one client. Meta's default setting gave the highest ROAS. Switching to 7-day click brought it down to something more believable. An incremental attribution read was lower again. Acquisition MER from the P&L, new customer revenue against total ad spend, was the most conservative and the closest to baseline. In a sale window the gaps get wider, because view-through and long windows soak up purchases that would have happened anyway. How to apply: 1) before the period starts, set reporting columns to 7-day click, or 7-day click and 1-day engaged view; 2) keep columns for the other settings next to each other and watch how the ratio between them moves day to day, rather than trusting any single number; 3) make budget calls against acquisition MER and contribution margin built from Shopify orders and your cost data; 4) for pre-season spend, add a post-treatment window so it does not get under-credited.
conditions: Meta accounts with enough purchase volume to compare settings; sale periods when view-through credit inflates results.
fails_when: Very low volume accounts where settings disagree mostly through noise; brands with no reliable new versus returning customer split to compute acquisition MER.
numbers: 7-day click or 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view during the sale

claim: Haus lift tests that ended three or more weeks before BFCM showed a 105% lift after spend stopped, and 41% of incremental value landed after the test window, so pre-season spend keeps paying into the sale.
body: Blue Sense cites the Haus Cyber Week incrementality report. Tests that finished at least three weeks before BFCM showed a 105% lift in the period after treatment ended; tests that finished closer to the sale showed 75%. Across the tests, 41% of the incremental value appeared only after the measured window had closed, and delayed effects during BFCM were close to three times those of normal periods. The delayed share differs by category: the figures shown were 93% for fashion and apparel against 30% for health, wellness, food and drink, so fashion brands are the most likely to under-read their pre-season spend. The practical meaning: holding back budget in September and October does not save ammunition for the sale, it shrinks the pool of people the sale can convert. How to apply: when you run a geo or holdout lift test, or read pre-season campaign results, keep measuring for several weeks after spend stops before you call the result. Judge pre-season campaigns on what they look like once the sale has booked, not on the day they run.
conditions: Brands with a big seasonal sale, most strongly fashion and apparel; based on Haus aggregate test data shown by Blue Sense, not one account.
fails_when: Brands with no sale event or a tiny awareness pool; short-consideration categories where delayed effects are small (the 30% health and food figure); lift tests too small to read.

+75% for tests ending closer to BFCM
41% of incremental value after the treatment window

claim: Reset ROAS targets for the discount: a store that breaks even at 2 ROAS needs about 4.5 after a 40% discount, because gross profit per order falls faster than price.
body: Most CAC allowances quietly assume normal gross profit per order. A sale cuts the price but not the cost of goods, shipping or payment fees, so gross profit per order drops by more than the discount percentage, and the ROAS you need to break even, or to hit a margin target, rises steeply as discount depth grows. Blue Sense's example: break-even ROAS of 2 at full price becomes about 4.5 at 40% off. The exact figure depends on your cost mix, so model it rather than copying it. How to apply: list every offer you might run. For each, recompute contribution margin per order after the discount, then the break-even ROAS and the target ROAS for the CM3 you want, and put those targets in the pacing sheet before the sale starts. Share real margin and discount figures with whoever runs your ads; without them nobody can tell you what efficiency to aim for. Check stock and cash before you choose depth: what you can afford to discount depends on what you need to clear and how much cash you need back.
conditions: Any store running a percentage discount with paid acquisition; the 2 to 4.5 figure is Blue Sense's example, not a fixed table.
fails_when: Gift with purchase or bundle offers, where cost per order changes in a different way; sales run mainly to clear dead stock, where a lower margin target can be justified.
numbers: break-even ROAS 2 at full price becomes about 4.5 with a 40% discount
asks: What ROAS do I need during a Black Friday discount?
How does a 40% discount change my break-even ROAS?
Why did we lose money on a sale that looked profitable in Ads Manager?
How deep can I discount for Black Friday?

claim: Scale on marginal cost, not averages: in one account, 25% more spend ($80,000) moved average cost per incremental customer from $337 to $392, while the extra spend cost over $1,000 per customer.
body: A blended average hides what the last dollar buys. In the account Blue Sense showed, baseline cost per incremental acquisition was $337. Adding 25% more spend, $80,000, lifted the blended figure only to $392, which looks fine, yet that extra $80,000 bought just 76 customers, a marginal cost above $1,000 each, about 2.5 times the blended number. Sale weekends make the mistake more likely: reporting looks best on the weekend and worst in the run-up, so teams shift budget into the weekend, which is where an extra dollar does the least. Blue Sense also warns that a simple revenue elasticity worked out from your own attributed data is an upper bound on the true response, so it can justify cuts but should not be used to justify scaling. How to apply: log spend and new customers (or contribution margin) by day, and divide the change in customers by the change in spend between spend levels. Compare that marginal cost to the most you can pay for a customer, not to your average CAC. Set your floor on contribution margin after ads (CM3), not ROAS, because revenue keeps climbing after profit has peaked. Treat the budget as a ceiling to deploy only while marginal returns hold.
conditions: Accounts spending enough that spend changes show up in daily customer counts; needs incrementality or new customer data.
fails_when: Small accounts where daily noise swamps the marginal read; spend that is building pre-season demand which books later, where a post-treatment window must be applied first.

+25% spend ($80,000) moved the average to $392
$80,000 bought 76 customers, over $1,000 each at the margin
about 2.5x gap hidden by the average

claim: Remove one-day view from your Meta attribution setting and use seven-day click plus one-day engaged view when reading ROAS or CPA.
body: One-day view credits a purchase to an ad when someone merely saw it, without clicking, and bought within a day. For brands with existing demand, many of those buyers would have bought anyway, so it inflates reported ROAS, especially on retargeting and bottom-funnel ads that are shown to people already about to buy. Blue Sense always strips one-day view out of the attribution models they read. Their setting: seven-day click and one-day engaged view, which counts purchases within a day of someone watching a meaningful part of a video ad without clicking. That keeps credit for video that genuinely engaged a viewer while dropping passive impressions. How to apply: in Ads Manager, use the compare attribution settings columns to see results under seven-day click, one-day view and one-day engaged view side by side. Set your reporting and, where you choose, the ad set attribution to seven-day click and one-day engaged view. Expect reported ROAS to drop; reset targets to the new basis rather than reading it as worse performance, and check it against blended new-customer cost.
conditions: Meta e-commerce accounts reading platform ROAS or CPA to make budget and creative decisions.
fails_when: Brands that have shown with lift tests that view-through purchases are incremental for them, such as heavy video brands in new categories; changing ad set attribution also changes what Meta optimises for.

claim: Tools like Triple Whale mostly reveal what basic hygiene fixes (unsegmented brand search, existing customers in prospecting, Meta view-throughs); after that, a $2K to $3K a month tool mainly anchors leadership on attributed numbers.
body: Nathan's view: much of the clarity people get from third-party attribution comes from accounts that never split out brand campaigns, never excluded existing customers and never moved Meta to 7-day click. The tool then shows that Google is really around 4x, not 20x. Segmenting campaigns properly gives that clarity for free. After the clean-up, what is left is a reporting dashboard costing about $2,000 to $3,000 a month that trains the C-suite to think in attributed ROAS and to divide credit between teams, such as email against paid, instead of thinking in new-customer revenue, total revenue lift and the incremental return on more spend. He was arguing this with a large retailer that wanted the tool as its single source of truth. Michael adds that on his clients who use such tools, the tool usually makes his own results look better, and with several models on offer it is unclear which to believe. How to apply: before buying or renewing an attribution tool, separate brand search, exclude past customers from prospecting and report Meta on click windows; then judge channels on spend against total and new-customer revenue over time.
conditions: Brands evaluating or paying for multi-touch attribution software.
fails_when: The account cannot be restructured soon and needs a temporary cross-check, or the tool is used only for operational reporting and not budget decisions.

claim: At about 60% of Blue Sense brands, customers acquired on a heavy discount have much worse LTV, so cohort your customers by the discount code used before scaling discount-led acquisition.
body: When you drop prices for Black Friday, end of financial year or another event, you reach people who were not buying because of price. When prices return to normal, many of them do not come back. Blue Sense sees worse repeat rates for discount-acquired cohorts at roughly 60% of the brands they work with, though some nine-figure retailers show no such effect, which is why you must check your own data. The trap is that the ad platforms make discounting look great: ROAS, efficiency and new customer volume all rise. Only the offer economics and the later value of those customers show the full picture. How to apply: export orders with discount codes, tag each customer by the code (or none) on their first order, and compare 90 and 365 day gross profit per customer and repeat rate between groups. If discounted cohorts are clearly worse, lower the CAC you are willing to pay during sales, or shift the event offer to bundles and gifts that hold margin.
conditions: Brands that run regular sale events or use first-order discount codes, with at least a few cohorts of history.
fails_when: Brands where discount buyers repeat as well as full-price buyers, as at some of the large retailers Blue Sense mentions.
numbers: about 60% of Blue Sense brands see worse LTV on discount-acquired customers

claim: Compute first-order gross profit as new-customer AOV minus COGS, shipping, fulfilment or 3PL, transaction fees and refunds; put refunds in LTGP, not CAC, and use real order data monthly.
body: CAC is total media spend across all channels divided by new customers in the period; look at it weekly or monthly for six to eight figure brands, and daily or hourly only at nine to ten figures. The other side, day-zero LTGP, should include every variable cost so that LTGP minus CAC is a true contribution margin: start from new-customer AOV, subtract cost of goods, cost of delivery (shipping, fulfilment, 3PL handling or pick and pack) and transaction fees. Then the one most people miss: refunds. If 20 of 100 new customers refund, common in fashion, you really acquired 80 paying ones. Blue Sense puts the refund adjustment on the LTGP side, not CAC, because refunds come from product quality; mixing them into CAC sends the media team chasing a problem it did not cause. Do not estimate LTGP as AOV times an assumed margin (for example $110 times 80%); the figure moves a lot by cohort, especially in discount months. How to apply: compute it from order-level data each month and refresh CAC targets from it.
conditions: Any brand setting CAC targets from unit economics.
numbers: 20 of 100 new customers refunding leaves 80 paying

claim: Extend the LTGP window only if the higher CAC buys real volume: if raising CAC from $40 to $50 adds 30% to 40% more new customers and you have the cash, do it; if it adds few, stay first-order profitable.
body: A longer LTGP window raises your CAC ceiling, but the ceiling is only worth raising if the platforms give you many more customers at it. Blue Sense frames it as a curve: new customers on one axis, CAC on the other. Higher CAC tolerance lets you win more auctions and reach colder people, so volume rises with diminishing returns. The decision is how steep your curve is between your two candidate targets. If moving from a $40 to a $50 CAC (30-day versus 90-day window) adds 30% to 40% more new customers, the business can grow about that much, provided you can fund the ad spend and inventory while waiting for payback. If $10 more CAC adds almost nothing, you are just paying more for the same buyers, and you should stay profitable on the first purchase. How to apply: raise the CAC target in steps for two to four weeks at a time, record new customers per week at each level, and keep the higher level only where the extra customers per extra dollar justify it.
conditions: Brands with room to scale spend and enough cash to fund a longer payback.
fails_when: Small or saturated audiences where higher bids add little volume, or cash-constrained brands that cannot fund the gap.
numbers: $40 versus $50 CAC target
30% to 40% more new customers as the case for extending

claim: Find your CAC floor as lowest sensible CPC divided by highest realistic conversion rate ($0.70 / 3% = $23); compare it with today's ($1 / 2% = $50) before promising cuts.
body: LTGP to CAC has two sides, and owners need to know how far each can move. Blue Sense finds inexperienced operators overestimate how low CAC can go and underestimate how much LTGP can rise through better front-end offers, bundles, subscriptions and retention. CAC can be bounded with a simple identity: CAC equals CPC divided by conversion rate. Set the best case using the lowest CPC you would accept before traffic turns to junk and the highest conversion rate you could plausibly reach. In their example, $0.70 divided by 3% gives a floor of about $23. The realistic case uses today's numbers: $1 CPC and a 2% conversion rate on a good day give $50. So the room to cut CAC lies between $23 and $50, and you should not plan to go much above $50. CPC itself is a weak metric except at the extremes: very high is bad, very low usually means poor traffic. How to apply: build this best and realistic band for CAC, do the same for 90 to 365 day LTGP, and decide which side has more room before allocating time and money.
conditions: Brands deciding between acquisition and retention investments, with stable CPC and conversion history.
fails_when: Channel mix or offer changes a lot (for example a new channel with very different CPCs), so past CPC and conversion bounds no longer apply.
numbers: CAC = CPC / conversion rate
floor: $0.70 / 3% = about $23
realistic: $1 / 2% = $50

claim: In CPG and supplements you often lose money on the first order ($50 CAC against $45 gross profit), so track CAC payback: the day repeat gross profit covers the gap.
body: Consumables are hard to acquire profitably on the first order. Blue Sense's example: $50 to acquire a customer against $45 gross profit on the first purchase, a $5 loss per new buyer. That is fine only because consumables and subscriptions repeat: people use the product up and reorder if they like it, so second, third and fourth orders are likely. The key metric becomes CAC payback period, the number of days until cumulative gross profit from a cohort equals what you paid to acquire it; every order after that is profit. Retention work that pulls second orders forward shortens payback and frees cash for more acquisition. How to apply: from your cohort table, find the first day when cumulative gross profit per customer is at least CAC, for each monthly cohort. Track it monthly. If payback stretches (for example after a discount-heavy month), slow spend or fix the offer; if it shortens, you can raise CAC targets. Make sure you have the cash to fund the gap before you accept a first-order loss.
conditions: Consumables, supplements and subscription brands with high repeat rates.
fails_when: Low-repeat categories, where a first-order loss is never recovered; or brands without the cash to carry losses until payback.

claim: Never quote LTV without a time window; measure lifetime gross profit (not revenue) at 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365 days by cohort.
body: In software, lifetime value and lifetime gross profit are nearly the same because the cost of serving a customer is tiny. In ecommerce, revenue hides product, shipping and fulfilment costs that vary by brand, so Blue Sense always talks about lifetime gross profit (LTGP). The second fix is time. 'What is your LTV?' has no answer unless you say over what period: few brands have existed long enough to know a true lifetime figure, and a 70-year or even three-year number does not help you pay for ads today. Say '180-day LTGP' instead. For example, a customer might bring $60 gross profit and $40 contribution margin on the first order; the question is what that grows to by day 180 on average across cohorts. How to apply: build a cohort table by acquisition month with cumulative gross profit per customer at day 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365, and use the window that matches your cash position when setting targets. Use real order-level costs, not a flat margin guess.
conditions: Any brand setting acquisition targets or judging retention work.
fails_when: Very young brands without enough history for 180 or 365 day cohorts; use 30 and 60 day figures and update as cohorts mature.
numbers: LTGP windows at 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365 days
example first order: $60 gross profit, $40 contribution margin

claim: Set the CAC target as LTGP divided by your target ratio (about 2): $80 30-day LTGP gives a $40 target; using $100 90-day LTGP gives $50, 25% more headroom.
body: Pick a window first. For most brands Blue Sense recommends basing targets on 30-day LTGP; repeat-friendly niches like supplements and some fashion can use 90 days. Longer windows let you spend more now and earn it back later, but the choice depends on your cash and appetite for loans or investors. Blue Sense dislikes debt-fuelled aggressive growth below roughly $15 to $20 million a year, because modelling interest against slow paybacks takes a skilled operator. Then pick the ratio. Under 1 you lose money in the window. 1 to 2 is inefficient: each ad dollar returns about $1.50 of gross profit before operating costs, so holding a good EBITDA margin is hard, though some well-funded clients chasing an exit run there. 2 to 3 is the scaling zone. Above 3 you are leaving growth on the table. Divide LTGP by the ratio: with $80 30-day LTGP and a target of 2, CAC target is $40; on $100 90-day LTGP it is $50, a 25% higher ceiling. How to apply: recompute the target monthly from fresh cohort LTGP and give it to the media buyer as the blended new-customer CAC ceiling.
conditions: Brands with reliable cohort gross profit data; Blue Sense mostly applies this to AU and US brands at $1M to $50M a year.
fails_when: LTGP data is missing or guessed; or cash is too tight to carry a 90-day payback even when the ratio looks fine.
numbers: ratio bands: under 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3+
$1 of spend returning about $1.50 gross profit at a 1.5 ratio
$80 / 2 = $40 CAC target
$100 / 2 = $50 CAC target
25% higher CAC ceiling with the 90-day window
avoid debt-led growth under about $15M to $20M a year

claim: Shopify's percentage of returning customers is not a repeat rate: it rises as a brand ages and when acquisition weakens, so it rewards buying fewer new customers.
body: The returning customer percentage at the top of Shopify analytics is returning-customer orders divided by all orders in the period. Two things swing it that have nothing to do with how well you keep customers. First, the age of the business: a 15-year-old brand has a huge past customer base, so more of today's orders come from it, and the number drifts up as any brand matures. Second, acquisition strength: if you win fewer first-time buyers, the share of returning orders rises and the metric looks better. Judging retention on it can push a team to under-invest in acquisition. Blue Sense says the only real use is slicing results during a sale to see whether it landed with new or existing customers. How to apply: replace it with cohort metrics, the share of each month's new customers who place a second order within 90 days, and cumulative gross profit per customer at 30, 90 and 365 days.
conditions: Any Shopify store using the default analytics dashboard.
numbers: returning customer % = returning orders / total orders

claim: Two brands with the same $40 CAC differ hugely if one grows first-order gross profit 30% by day 90 and the other 12%; the first can let CAC rise to $45 and still earn more.
body: Retention matters for paid media because it sets how much you can afford to pay for a customer. In the Blue Sense example both brands pay $40 to acquire a customer and make $100 gross profit on the first order. Brand A's customers are worth $112 by day 90; brand B's are worth $130. On a 90-day view brand B earns roughly 10% to 15% more profit per customer, so it can bid harder, raise budgets and let CAC climb to $45 while still beating brand A. More spend at a higher CAC buys more customers, which compounds. How to apply: compute your own 90-day gross profit lift (90-day gross profit per customer divided by first-order gross profit) from a cohort report. Every point of lift you add is extra CAC headroom you can hand to the media buyer. When deciding between a retention project and an acquisition project, express both in gross profit per customer over the same window so they can be compared.
conditions: Brands with some repeat purchasing and a paid acquisition program limited by CAC targets.
fails_when: One-time purchase categories (furniture, big appliances) with almost no repeat buying in 90 days, where first-order gross profit is the whole story.

claim: A higher AOV country is less ahead than it looks once variable costs land: in the example US orders carried $43 of variable costs against $28 in Australia, so do not cut the lower AOV market.
body: In Valentin's example the US collected far more per order, but variable costs (cost of goods, carrier and fulfilment, payment fees and refunds) were about $43 per order there against about $28 in Australia, a $15 gap. After those costs the profit gap between the two markets shrank sharply. Looking only at order value, you would pour money into the US and neglect Australia; after costs, the US is still better but not by much, ending around 4.4% profit on order value after acquisition. Volume matters too: multiply profit contribution per order by orders to get total contribution dollars per market. A country with weaker unit economics can still deliver a large share of profit dollars, so you would not shut it down. How to apply it: rank markets on contribution dollars, then on contribution per order, never on AOV alone. In the example the order was the US first for further investment, Australia second with optimisation, and New Zealand needing acquisition fixes before more budget.
conditions: Multi-country brands comparing markets for budget or expansion decisions.
fails_when: Markets where costs are shared and hard to split by order; single month snapshots in seasonal businesses.
numbers: variable costs per order: US about $43 vs AU about $28
$15 per order gap
US profit about 4.4% of order value after acquisition

Should we cut a country with lower margins?
How do I rank which markets to invest in?
What costs should I include per order by country?

claim: Budget payment processing per country: about 2.5 to 3.5% for domestic cards, about 4 to 5% when Shopify converts a foreign currency, and 5 to 6.5% where buy now pay later and conversion stack up.
body: Payment fees are easy to treat as one flat number, but they differ by market. Valentin's ranges: domestic card transactions without international fees typically cost 2.5 to 3.5%. When the order is in a foreign currency that Shopify converts, the markup pushes it to around 4 to 5%. Heavy use of buy now pay later adds more, so a market combining BNPL, currency conversion and the Shopify gateway can sit at 5 to 6.5%. For an Australian brand selling in US dollars, money eventually has to be converted back, and doing that through Shopify is expensive; cheaper conversion services exist. How to apply it: in your country table, set a payment fee rate per column from your actual payout reports rather than one blended rate. Multiply it by order value to get a dollar cost per order. If a foreign market shows 5% or more, price the gap against a lower cost conversion option or a local payment setup, and check how much of that market pays with BNPL.
conditions: Brands selling in more than one currency or offering buy now pay later.
fails_when: Single currency stores with no BNPL; rates change by provider and plan, so check your own statements.
numbers: domestic: about 2.5 to 3.5%
Shopify currency conversion: about 4 to 5%
BNPL plus conversion plus gateway: about 5 to 6.5%

claim: Build unit economics per country as a table with one column per geography and per order rows down to profit contribution; beyond Shopify exports it needs cost of goods, carrier and 3PL fees, and ad spend by location.
body: Unit economics is the profit and loss turned into a single order. Valentin's model puts each geography in its own column (for example Australia, US, New Zealand, other) and lists the per order metrics down the rows: revenue per session, conversion rate, orders, unit price, units per order, discount, shipping and duties collected, refunds, cost of goods, carrier and fulfilment, payment fees, gross profit, CAC and profit contribution. Shopify exports cover sessions, orders, prices, units and discounts. Three more inputs are needed. Cost of goods: best is Shopify's cost per item exported by country; next, an inventory system report by country; last resort, average unit cost times units per order (1.8 units at $8 is $14.40). Carrier and fulfilment: a ShipStation report by country, your 3PL's export, or carrier invoices (DHL for express from Australia to the US); if you pack in-house, spread labour over orders, such as $10,000 a month across 1,900 orders, about $5 each. Ad spend by location: from separate ad accounts or location breakdowns; Blue Sense says you can pull it from reports even when the account structure is messy. Split the other column into any country with material volume.
conditions: Shopify brands selling into several countries with enough orders per country to average.
fails_when: Single country brands; countries with only a handful of orders, where averages swing wildly.
numbers: example COGS estimate: 1.8 units x $8 = $14.40
in-house fulfilment example: $10,000 a month / 1,900 orders = about $5 per order

Where do I get shipping costs by country?
How do I calculate COGS by country in Shopify?

claim: Revenue per session by country, net revenue excluding tax divided by Shopify sessions, shows where traffic earns most; in the example the US made $5.12 a session, Australia $4.27 and New Zealand $2.89.
body: Revenue per session folds conversion rate and order value into one number: how much net revenue each visit brings. Pull sessions from Shopify's sessions report with the dimension set to country, take net revenue by country with taxes removed, and divide. In Valentin's example the US earned $5.12 a session, Australia $4.27, New Zealand $2.89 and the other group about $1.50. Then read conversion rate separately, since the two can disagree: Australia converted best, the US less well, New Zealand about 1.6% and other countries about 0.6%. So the US earned most per visit through higher order values despite weaker conversion. Decision rule: if a country's unit economics look normal but its conversion rate lags, suspect the site; brands running a separate US store or theme should compare stores directly and fix the weaker one. Also split the other group into any country with real volume (UK, Canada, Singapore, Middle East). Middle East orders are often far larger than average, around $1,000, so isolate them or they distort the group.
conditions: Shopify stores with session and order data by country and enough traffic per country.
fails_when: Small countries with few sessions; Shopify session counts are estimates, so use them to compare, not as exact figures.
numbers: revenue per session: US $5.12, AU $4.27, NZ $2.89, other about $1.50
conversion rate: NZ about 1.6%, other about 0.6%
Middle East orders around $1,000

claim: Track average cart value, unit price times units per order minus discounts, apart from true AOV; when shipping and duties lift AOV well above cart value, expect more people to quit at checkout.
body: Valentin uses cart value for what a buyer carries before checkout: shelf prices, units per order and discounts, with no shipping, duties or refunds. True AOV is what you actually keep from the order after shipping and duties collected and after refunds. Shopify's dashboard AOV is gross sales minus discounts divided by orders, so it is really cart value: it leaves out shipping collected (Blue Sense estimates around 10% of revenue for most brands) and ignores refunds, which in fashion can make AOV look higher than it really is. Why the gap matters: the funnel has three steps, add to cart, start checkout and finish checkout. If cart value and AOV are close, there is little surprise at checkout. If shipping and duties push the total well above cart value, buyers see fees late and more abandon at checkout. How to apply it: calculate both per country. Where the gap is large, check checkout abandonment for that country in Shopify's funnel and test showing shipping and duties earlier, raising or lowering the free shipping threshold, or pricing duties into the product.
conditions: Stores that charge shipping or duties, especially in cross-border markets.
fails_when: Stores with free shipping and duty paid pricing everywhere, where cart value and AOV nearly match.
numbers: shipping collected about 10% of revenue for most brands (Blue Sense estimate)
3 funnel steps: add to cart, checkout started, checkout completed
asks: Why is my Shopify AOV different from what I actually earn per order?

claim: When comparing countries, allow for reversed seasons and local return habits: fashion return rates can run 50 to 100% higher in the US than Australia, and some clients see 3x US refund rates.
body: Two things distort country comparisons. Returns: Blue Sense says fashion brands entering the US should expect return rates 50 to 100% above home levels, and Valentin has clients whose US refund rate is three times their Australian one. American shoppers more often buy several items to try and send back, while Australians tend to order cautiously. New markets also bring fewer units per order and heavier discounting, because buyers do not trust an unknown brand yet. Together these mean each region needs its own marketing targets; a CAC that works at home may lose money abroad. Seasonality: for an Australian brand selling in the US, seasons are reversed. Valentin's example used May data, winter in Australia and the warm season in the US, which partly explained weaker Australian spending that month. How to apply it: set a refund allowance per country from your own returns data and include it in profit contribution. Set target CAC per country from that market's contribution, not the home one. Compare markets on the same season or year on year rather than one month side by side.
conditions: Brands selling in both hemispheres or entering the US, especially in fashion and apparel.
fails_when: Categories with low returns (consumables, supplements); markets in the same hemisphere and season.
numbers: fashion return rates about 50 to 100% higher in a new US market
some clients: about 3x refund rate in the US
example month: May (AU winter, US warm season)

claim: Work out two profit contributions per country, gross profit minus blended CAC and gross profit minus new customer CAC; break-even on new customers is fine only where repeat orders carry it.
body: Blended CAC is ad spend in a country divided by all orders there; new customer CAC is the same spend divided by new customer orders only. Subtract each from gross profit per order to get blended and new profit contribution. In Valentin's example (real client numbers, altered for privacy): Australia was close to break-even on new customers, but about 55% of orders came from repeat customers, so blended contribution matched the US. New Zealand lost about $13 on every new customer, with new customer CAC around $75 against $62 in Australia, though repeats lifted blended contribution to about $24 per order. The US earned the most total profit. The decisions: keep acquiring in Australia at break-even because retention pays it back; do not scale New Zealand until acquisition improves, since adding budget to a loss-making acquisition can spiral; and look for more in the US, including better conversion, which lowers new customer CAC. How to apply it: build both rows per country, check the repeat share next to them, and bring the table to your media partner to ask whether a market is saturated or still has room.
conditions: Brands with meaningful repeat purchase rates and ad spend that can be split by country.
fails_when: Brands with little repeat buying, where blended CAC flatters acquisition; a single month's data, which can mislead in seasonal markets.
numbers: Australia repeat share about 55%
New Zealand: about $13 loss per new customer
new customer CAC: about $75 NZ vs $62 AU
NZ blended contribution about $24 per order
NZ repeat share about 48%

claim: A five minute first check splits revenue into conversion rate, order value and sessions, compares true business numbers with attributed ones, and checks the dip against the seasonal forecast.
body: Before going into any ad account, work out what actually fell. Revenue equals conversion rate times average order value times sessions. If conversion rate fell, look at the website. If sessions fell, find which traffic source lost clicks. If order value fell, look at which products are being pushed (Google may suddenly favour cheaper items) or whether an upsell or cross sell on the site changed. Next, separate true business numbers (revenue, contribution profit, MER) from attributed platform numbers. A dip only in attributed numbers may be conversion lag or broken tracking, not lost sales. If true revenue fell, see which platform's attributed numbers fell with it: if Meta ROAS dropped from 4 to 3 at the same moment, Meta is the likely cause. Finally compare the dip to your seasonal forecast. If the fall matches what last year and the forecast predicted, stop: there is nothing to fix. Without a forecast, normal seasonal swings can eat hours of pointless diagnosis. Blue Sense says a skilled buyer finishes this level in about five minutes, and often the search ends here.
conditions: Stores with Shopify or similar data on sessions, conversion rate and order value, and ideally a monthly revenue forecast by season.
fails_when: Very new brands with no history to forecast against, where seasonality cannot yet be separated from real change.
numbers: revenue = conversion rate x average order value x sessions
level one takes about 5 minutes
example: Meta ROAS falling from 4 to 3

claim: Above $200k a month, fashion brands need geolift testing, store deduplication, daily P&L reconciliation, 200 plus new ads a month and at least 10% of ad spend going into creative production.
body: Blue Sense's top-tier list. Measurement: geolift tests in place, omnichannel deduplication of new customers, and day-by-day and month-by-month reconciliation so every account decision ties to P&L results; track contribution margin on first-time and on existing customers separately. Meta: the account becomes complex because the business is, with several units and markets, and the structure should mirror that. Channels: add TikTok if you have the native content to feed it, and consider YouTube as a top-of-funnel channel. YouTube is hard to measure, so it only makes sense once you can run geolift tests and fund it with a large budget, which is why it belongs at this tier. Creative: 200 plus new ads a month, sized to the expected value of each ad, and at least 10% of ad spend going into production, since brands at this level often let production lag spend. Scaling: go international once local online revenue is above about 10M.
conditions: Fashion brands spending over about $200k a month across paid channels.
fails_when: Brands that reach this spend through one hero product and one market, where much of the complexity is not needed.

at least 10% of ad spend on creative production

claim: Adjust CAC for returns: a $200 order at 50% margin and $50 CAC looks like a 2.0 first-purchase payback, but a 50% return rate doubles real CAC to $100 and the ratio to 1.0.
body: A common fashion mistake is to compare first-order gross profit with CAC and stop there. Blue Sense's example: $200 average order, 50% gross margin, so $100 gross profit, and a $50 CAC, giving a 2.0 ratio that looks healthy. If half of those orders are returned and those buyers never come back, you really paid $50 for each of 100 orders but kept only 50 customers, so CAC is $100 and the ratio is 1.0. The same cut applies to ROAS: a fashion account with 50% returns is delivering half the impact its platform ROAS suggests, and acquisition MER and contribution must all be net of returns. How to apply: pull your return rate by month and by product type. Divide reported CAC by one minus the return rate to get return-adjusted CAC, and set KPIs on that figure. Extend the LTV window far enough to include the returns period.
conditions: Apparel and footwear brands with meaningful return rates, typically 20% to 50% plus.
fails_when: Low-return categories, or brands where most returns become exchanges rather than refunds.

50% return rate makes CAC $100 and the ratio 1.0
