claim: Before using gross margin in fashion ad targets, decide whether it is full-price margin or the blended margin after sale markdowns, and charge burnt or donated stock against it.
body: Most fashion brands push slow stock to a sale page, so the margin you plug into CAC or ROAS targets matters. Full-price margin can be far above the average margin once grade B and C stock sells at markdown. If you set paid targets on full-price margin while much of what sells is discounted, the targets are too loose. If stock is never sold, but donated, destroyed or written off, that cost belongs against average gross profit too, even though no sale shows it. How to apply: ask finance for three numbers for the last two seasons: full-price gross margin, blended gross margin including markdowns, and the value of stock written off or given away as a share of revenue. Use the blended figure net of write-offs for account-level targets. Use full-price margin only for campaigns that sell full-price ranges, and the markdown margin for clearance campaigns.
conditions: Fashion and seasonal brands that run regular sales or clear stock outside of sales.
fails_when: Brands that rarely discount and sell through nearly all stock, where full-price and blended margins are close.
asks: Which gross margin should I use to set my ad targets?
How do markdowns affect my break even ROAS?
Should written off stock count in my margin?

claim: Do not pour fashion ad spend into a product already selling fast; in Blue Sense's example, 90% of $100k on the viral SKU cut its contribution margin from $500k to $410k.
body: Ad accounts drift to the product with the best ROAS, and in fashion that is often one that went viral and would sell anyway. Blue Sense's worked example: three products, 10,000 units each, $100k monthly budget. Product A sells through in about 50 days at a 7x ROAS; B in about 75 days at 4.4x; C, a flop, in about 240 days at 2.5x. Put $90k behind A and it sells out in about 9 days instead of 50, but its purchase order still yields $500k gross profit (on $1M revenue at 50% margin), now minus $90k of ads, so contribution falls to about $410k. You paid to speed up a sale you already had. Spend on B and C instead: their ROAS is lower, but B might clear in 30 days and C drop to 100 days of stock, so far less goes to markdown. How to apply: add a days-of-inventory column next to ROAS for each product or ad. Hold spend on products already clearing fast, and steer budget to stock that will not sell on its own.
conditions: Fashion and apparel brands buying fixed runs of stock per product, where one viral product would sell through without ads.
fails_when: The fast seller is a replenishable core line where speeding sales lets you reorder sooner, or ads on it bring new customers with high LTV that the margin maths ignores.

A: about 50 days of inventory, 7x ROAS; B: about 75 days, 4.4x; C: about 240 days, 2.5x
90% of budget on A cuts it to about 9 days

claim: Fashion brands over-attribute badly: one nine-figure brand showed 36x Meta ROAS, 17x on 7-day click, 8.22x on incremental attribution, against an 8x acquisition MER.
body: Older fashion brands get 30% to 75% of revenue from returning customers, so view-through credit and clicks from people who would have bought anyway inflate platform numbers. Blue Sense's audits of two multi-nine-figure fashion brands: Brand A showed 36x ROAS over 30 days in Ads Manager, 17x on 7-day click, 8.22x on incremental attribution, and an acquisition MER (new customer revenue over total ad spend) of 8x. Brand B showed 13.6x, then 8.6x, then 5.16x, against a 4.4x acquisition MER. The incremental number, which uses holdout groups to see who would have bought without ads, lined up with the business's real figure; the default view was about three times off. How to apply: in Ads Manager choose Columns, then Compare attribution settings, and add 7-day click and incremental attribution. Make budget calls on the view that is closest to your acquisition MER, and treat any platform ROAS far above it as a warning.
conditions: Established fashion and CPG brands with high returning-customer revenue share.
fails_when: Young brands with mostly new-customer revenue, where default and incremental reads are closer.

claim: In Australia, run geolift tests on commuting zones instead of states; there are about 60 plus, and each holds only one or two stores, so store sales can be tied to spend changes.
body: Australia has too few states for a clean state-level geolift, and store-heavy retailers make it worse. A typical large fashion retailer might have about 10 stores in New South Wales, seven or eight in Victoria, about six in Queensland and one each in the smaller states. A state-level test would have to read lift across many stores whose sales swing with ranging and local weather that week. Blue Sense uses commuting zones instead: areas where people both live and work and rarely cross the boundary. There are about 60 plus in Australia, which gives far more choice for building matched control and treatment groups, and each zone usually holds only one or two stores. That lets you measure in-store revenue against a spend change much more tightly. How to apply: map your store locations and online orders to commuting zones, pair zones with similar revenue patterns, raise spend in the treatment zones only, and compare store plus online revenue against control.
conditions: Australian omnichannel brands with stores in several regions and enough spend to move regional revenue.
fails_when: Online-only brands with little regional spread, or budgets too small to shift a zone's revenue.
numbers: about 60 plus commuting zones in Australia
each zone usually holds 1 to 2 stores

claim: Judge fashion paid media on 180-day LTV to CAC; good fashion brands add about 15% to gross profit from repeat buyers by day 90 and about 55% by day 365.
body: First-purchase maths breaks in fashion because returns land weeks after the sale and repeat buying changes a lot from brand to brand in the first six months. Blue Sense uses gross profit LTV over 180 days divided by CAC as the main health metric. Benchmarks for a good fashion brand: gross profit per customer grows about 15% from repeat purchases by day 90, and about 55% by day 365. If your cohorts fall short, you must acquire customers more cheaply up front, because the back end will not rescue you. Their playbook target for brands spending $30k to $75k a month is a 180-day LTGP to CAC of about 2 to 3. How to apply: build monthly cohorts in Shopify or your analytics tool, calculate gross profit per customer net of returns at day 90, 180 and 365, and compare with the benchmarks. Set your allowed CAC from the 180-day number, not from first order gross profit.
conditions: Fashion and apparel brands with at least 90 to 180 days of customer cohorts and returns that land weeks after the sale.
fails_when: Very new brands without 90 to 180 days of cohort history; use the benchmarks as placeholders until real cohorts exist.
numbers: day 90: about 15% gross profit lift from repeat buyers
day 365: about 55% gross profit lift
target 180-day LTGP to CAC about 2 to 3 at $30k to $75k a month spend

claim: Omnichannel brands should dedupe online first-time buyers against store customers; in one case Shopify-based CAC read $70 while true new-customer CAC was $100, and both converged near $80 after excluding store buyers.
body: If stores and the website run on separate systems, someone who bought in a store and later orders online shows up in Shopify as a first-time customer. That flatters CAC and acquisition MER and lets cold campaigns target people you already have. Where a client has a customer data platform joining store and online records, Blue Sense tracks two numbers: normal new customer CAC (Shopify first-time customers over ad spend) and true new customer CAC (customers new to both store and online, over ad spend). In one account the first was about $70 and the second about $100. They then excluded all store customers from cold campaigns using the deduplicated list. The Shopify-based CAC crept up while true CAC fell, and both met around $80, because far more spend now reached truly new people. How to apply: if you have stores, build a joined customer list, upload it as an exclusion for prospecting, and report true CAC beside Shopify CAC.
conditions: Brands with physical retail or wholesale-to-consumer channels whose customers are not on Shopify POS.
fails_when: Pure online brands, or brands already using one POS and customer record across channels.

deduplicated true new customer CAC about $100
both converged near $80 after excluding store customers

claim: Prove Meta or TikTok lift with a geolift test: cluster US states whose revenue moves together, raise spend only in the treatment group, and read the gap; Kookai's US test showed clear lift and justified scaling.
body: At large scale, and for brands with stores, platform attribution becomes unreliable, and the question is often how media lifts store and marketplace revenue as well as the website. Geolift tests answer this. Method: take historical revenue and order data by state and use a clustering algorithm to pair states whose revenue moves together, for example one group as control and another as treatment. Before the test, the groups track so tightly you can predict one from the other. Then change one thing in the treatment group only, such as adding TikTok at $100k a month or a big Meta budget increase, and measure how far treatment revenue pulls away from what the control predicts. When Blue Sense took over Kookai's US market, a base level of revenue seemed unrelated to ads. After restructuring, they raised budget sharply in one test state and saw large lift against control, which gave them the confidence to scale the US quickly. They then used the same method to check TikTok as it was added.
conditions: Brands spending enough in a market to shift state-level revenue, typically $200k plus a month in total ad spend.
fails_when: Small budgets that cannot move regional revenue, or markets where regions do not track each other well.
numbers: example treatment: TikTok at $100k a month in the test states

claim: Set a higher acquisition MER target for November and December than for January; holiday buyers return more and repeat less, and Blue Sense has seen 80% to 100% return rates in discount periods.
body: Customers acquired in January to March tend to return less and grow more in lifetime value. Customers acquired in November and December return much more and are worth less, because they are discount driven, many orders are gifts, and loose return policies let people buy ten items, try them on, and send most back. Blue Sense has seen brands in international markets with 80% to 100% return rates during discount periods, meaning almost all of that revenue was refunded. So an acquisition MER (new customer revenue divided by total ad spend) of 4 in January is far better than a 4 in November. How to apply: before peak season, pull last year's return rate and 90-day repeat rate for holiday cohorts versus Q1 cohorts. Raise the holiday aMER target by enough to cover the extra returns and lower LTV. Review your returns policy too, since a generous one can attract serial returners.
conditions: Fashion and gift-heavy brands with a strong sale season and meaningful returns.
fails_when: Brands with final-sale policies or low return rates, or where holiday buyers prove to repeat as well as others in your own cohort data.
numbers: 80% to 100% return rates seen in discount periods in some international markets
example: aMER of 4 in Jan and Feb vs 4 in Nov and Dec are not equal

claim: Set peak-season paid targets backward from net profit: add opex to get a contribution target, then work out revenue (capped by stock) and ad efficiency, net of expected returns and lower LTV.
body: Blue Sense sets KPIs from the bottom of the P&L up, not from a ROAS habit. Steps for a period like November and December: 1) Agree the net profit target for the period. 2) Add planned operating expenses to get the contribution profit you need. 3) Work out what revenue at what ad efficiency produces that contribution, and check it against the stock you actually have, since inventory caps revenue. 4) Turn that into the monthly efficiency target, such as acquisition MER, and adjust it for the return rate and the weaker LTV you expect from that season's buyers. How to apply: build this in a simple sheet with stock on hand per range, expected return rate and expected repeat rate as inputs, so changing one input updates the target. Share the final target with whoever runs ads before the period starts, so they buy toward profit rather than toward last year's ROAS.
conditions: Brands with a monthly P&L and stock data that can be shared with the ads team.

claim: Track two versions of acquisition MER in fashion, raw and with returns added back; refunds processed in batches create fake dips, and hitting one but not the other points to returns.
body: Acquisition MER is net new customer revenue divided by total ad spend across all platforms. In fashion it can mislead day to day, because many teams process refunds in bulk on certain days. The raw line looks stable, then plunges, and people waste hours hunting for a platform change, a conversion rate drop or a traffic dip that never happened. Blue Sense built custom metrics with two versions of every core number: the plain version and an adjusted version that adds returns back. If the adjusted aMER holds steady while raw aMER dips, the dip was refund processing, not ad performance. If you hit the adjusted target but miss the raw one, returns are the problem, and the next step is to find which products drove them. How to apply: in your dashboard, add a returns-added-back version of aMER and CAC, set targets on both, and check both daily.
conditions: Brands with significant returns and refunds processed in batches.
fails_when: Brands with few returns or refunds posted to the original order date, where one series is enough.

claim: IM8 grows on the risk lever: in Q2 2026 it spent $35.7M on marketing against $45M revenue (EBITDA minus $18.6M), funded by a $1B facility lending up to 70% of marketing spend against a 6-month payback.
body: IM8 has product (a multivitamin repositioned into many angles), talent (David Beckham at launch) and global distribution, but its standout lever is risk. In the second quarter of 2026 it did about $45 million of revenue and spent $35.7 million on marketing, about 79% of revenue, giving EBITDA of minus $18.6 million in the quarter, a run rate near minus $100 million a year on roughly $200 million of revenue. That only works because its customers repay acquisition cost in about six months. To fund it, IM8 uses a credit facility of up to $1 billion that lends up to 70% of marketing spend (spend $100, borrow $70), repaid from returning customer revenue, with the company guaranteeing the loan in full. The shareholder letter says capital was its bottleneck and this removes it; its next lever is cohort quality, because the facility depends on cohorts paying back. How to apply: never copy a brand's spend level without knowing how it is funded. If you consider acquisition financing, you need reliable cohort data, a payback you can prove, and acceptance that weak cohorts become your debt.

fails_when: Brands without stable cohort history; one-off purchase products; owners unwilling to guarantee debt.

claim: Opening a store in a new area lifts online sales there, because shoppers try on in store and buy online later; Alo grew from 12 to over 150 stores in three years, which also inflates its Meta numbers.
body: Alo Yoga's main lever is distribution: it went from about 12 stores in 2020 to more than 150 in roughly three years, and it pairs stores with celebrities and creators. Blue Sense's point is that in fashion especially, a new store in an area without one raises online revenue nearby. People try products on, then buy online later because a size is out of stock, the store's size run is broken, or they want time to think. Those shoppers then visit the website and get retargeted, so Meta takes credit and Alo's ads look stronger than they are. How to apply: if you sell through your own stores, pop-ups or retail partners, compare online sales by postcode or region before and after each opening against similar areas without one, and credit stores with that lift when judging them. Expect Meta's reported results to improve around openings and do not raise budgets on that alone. If you are studying a store-led brand, look at where and how it opens stores and uses creators, not its ads.

claim: Trust Meta ROAS more the higher you go: ad level is weak, ad set is better, and campaign ROAS on 7-day click with existing customers excluded tracks the real P&L closely.
body: Because Meta sequences several ads before a sale and credits the last click, ad-level ROAS mostly tells you which ad closed, not which ad worked. At the ad set level the sequence is mostly contained, because Meta prefers to serve ads from the same ad set to the same person, so the group number is more honest. Some cross-serving between ad sets still happens, so one ad set can look better because it picks up buyers warmed by another; keeping one concept per ad set limits this. At the campaign level, with a 7-day click attribution setting and existing customers excluded, Blue Sense finds the number lines up with the P&L. How to apply: make scale, cut and budget calls on ad set and campaign numbers, and use ad-level numbers only as hints. Check your settings first: if the campaign counts 1-day view or does not exclude existing customers, it will overstate new customer results.
conditions: Prospecting campaigns set to 7-day click attribution with existing customers excluded.
fails_when: Campaigns that include existing customers or view-through attribution, or very small campaigns where noise dominates; still confirm with blended new customer cost or a holdout test.

claim: Do not judge upper-funnel statics by their own last-click ROAS: they rarely close the sale themselves, so a curiosity static missing your 7x bottom-funnel benchmark may still be driving the account.
body: Teams used to bottom-of-funnel statics are used to high in-platform returns, because those statics catch people who were already close to buying. When they start making true top-of-funnel statics, the new ads do not show anything like a 7x return, and the conclusion is that statics do not work for them or that they lack the skill. Blue Sense says that is usually wrong. A curiosity-driven static seldom gets the purchase at first touch; the buyer often converts later through a middle or bottom-of-funnel ad that takes the attributed credit. The upper-funnel static brought cheap reach and traffic that fed those other ads. So measure success and scale decisions against financial numbers such as new customer revenue, acquisition MER and blended results as spend shifts, not only in-platform metrics per ad. How to apply: when you add upper-funnel statics, track acquisition MER and new customer counts weekly for the account; judge the static on whether those hold or improve as it spends, and keep the attribution comparison columns in view.
conditions: Accounts running both upper-funnel and retargeting creative, with business-level KPIs available.
fails_when: Accounts where acquisition MER falls as upper-funnel statics spend; then the halo is not there and the ads are simply not working.

claim: For XYZ, compute each SKU's monthly coefficient of variation over 12 months (X under 10%, Y 10% to 25%, Z above 25% in Thieuleux's bands) and tune the bands to your own data.
body: ABC ranks SKUs by value; XYZ ranks them by how steady demand is. Coefficient of variation (CV) = standard deviation of monthly demand / average monthly demand, over the last 12 months (in a spreadsheet, STDEVP over AVERAGE). Thieuleux's worked example: one item has CV 5%, another 58%. His bands are X below 10%, Y 10% to 25%, Z above 25%, but he calls them arbitrary: if almost nothing lands in X, move the bands to natural breaks in your own CV list. Other guides use 0.5 and 1.0, which suit weekly data where CVs run higher; the bucket size changes the answer, so state it. A blind spot he flags: CV treats a predictable seasonal peak as noise. A seasonal item and a sporadic one both scored about 52% to 54%, though the seasonal one is far easier to forecast. Fix it by computing CV on forecast errors (or using forecast accuracy) instead of raw sales. Steps: export 12 months of units per SKU, compute CV, set bands, then cross with ABC.
conditions: Ranges of roughly 50 or more SKUs with at least 12 months of history.
fails_when: Most SKUs are under a year old, or demand is strongly seasonal and CV is computed on raw sales rather than forecast errors.

claim: Give each ABC/XYZ cell its own stock policy: high service on A items with less safety stock for AX than AZ, lower service on C items, and question stocking CZ at all.
body: Crossing ABC (value) with XYZ (steadiness) gives nine cells, and each needs a different service target because safety stock cost rises fast with service level. Thieuleux's policy logic: A items drive the business, so set the highest service levels there; AX items are predictable, so they reach high service with little safety stock, while AZ items need more buffer for the same target. B items follow the same pattern a notch lower. CX items matter little and are stable, so a lower service level and small buffers are fine. CZ items, low value and unpredictable, are where he sees much of a company's sleeping stock, and his advice is a lower service level or not stocking them at all (make to order, pre-order, or drop). How to apply: pick a z value per cell (for example 2.05 for AX and AZ, 1.65 for B, 1.28 for CX, and no safety stock for CZ), apply it in the reorder point, and review cells each quarter. Use the matrix to explain to the team why not every SKU gets 99%.

fails_when: A C item is a traffic driver or a required add-on to an A item (a refill, a charger), so its stockout costs more than its own revenue suggests.

claim: Blanket SKU cuts of 24% to 91% per category cut an online grocer's total sales through fewer visits, and Walmart restored about 8,500 cut items in 2011; prune selectively and watch repeat rate.
body: The same research review shows the downside. Borle and colleagues (2005) studied an online grocery service that cut its assortment in every category at once, removing 24% to 91% of items per category. Total store sales fell, through both fewer visits and smaller baskets, and fewer visits did more damage. Less frequently bought categories were hurt most. Walmart cut thousands of marginal SKUs in 2009 to reduce clutter and improve supply chain efficiency, then after years of US sales declines announced in 2011 that it was bringing back about 8,500 items, with in-store signs saying they were back. The lesson for a store is that a cut can look fine inside the category while customers quietly shop less often. How to apply: cut in waves, not all at once; before each wave, list customers whose last two orders included a cut SKU and email them the closest alternative; after the wave, compare 60 and 90-day repeat rates and order frequency for those customers against similar customers who were not affected.
conditions: Stores planning large range reductions, especially in categories customers buy only occasionally.
fails_when: The cut SKUs had almost no repeat buyers, or a direct substitute is kept at the same price.

claim: Cutting redundant low sellers can hold or lift sales: an FMI test removed up to 54% of slow SKUs with no sales loss, but cutting a whole size or brand shoppers rely on backfires.
body: Kahn, Weingarten and Townsend review the evidence on pruning ranges. In a 1993 Food Marketing Institute experiment, supermarkets removed as much as 54% of low-selling SKUs with no loss of sales and sometimes a gain, because removing redundant items cut confusion. Boatwright and Nunes (2001), studying 42 frequently bought categories at an online grocer, found that cutting low sellers could raise category sales, but the effect depended on what was cut: shoppers reacted badly to losing size options, and positively to losing items that were redundant or unrelated to their favourite brands and flavours. Broniarczyk and colleagues found shoppers do not notice cuts as long as the shelf space stays the same and only low-preference items go, unless their own favourite is removed. How to apply: before cutting, group SKUs by attribute (size, colour, scent, pack). Cut duplicates within a group first, keep at least one option in every size or format customers buy, and keep the page or collection looking as full.
conditions: Ranges with many near-duplicate SKUs in frequently bought categories.
fails_when: The cut removes the only option in a size, format or price point that a group of loyal buyers depends on.

claim: Shopify reports profit only for variants that had a cost per item when they sold, and that cost is a static snapshot, so enter landed BOM cost before launch and update it per new PO.
body: Your BOM and landed cost only help margin decisions if they reach the store's reports. Shopify's profit reports work out gross profit as net sales minus cost, and gross margin as (net sales minus cost) divided by net sales, times 100. Two rules matter. First, a variant with no cost recorded when it sold is left out of the gross profit by product report, so missing costs make the report look complete when it is not. Second, the cost field is static: the report uses the figure that was there at the time, so profit history is only as good as how often you updated it. How to apply it: roll each SKU's BOM up to a landed cost per variant (factory price plus freight, duty and inbound fees per unit). Bulk edit or import that cost into every variant before launch. When a new purchase order arrives at a different cost, update the variants the day stock is received, and keep a dated cost log outside Shopify. Read margin in the report, not on the product page: discounts and refunds lower net sales, so report margins sit below the product page figure. Use the profit margin by order report when you need shipping, duties and import taxes charged to customers included.
conditions: Shopify stores using its built-in profit reports.
fails_when: Stores that run COGS in an inventory or accounting app that overrides Shopify's cost field, or other platforms.
numbers: Gross margin = (net sales - cost) / net sales x 100
Variants with no cost at sale are excluded from gross profit by product

claim: Promotions spill into other categories: complements gained about 20% of the bump and substitutes lost 11%, a net halo of about 9% of the item's own effect.
body: Leeflang and colleagues decomposed the promotion bump while counting effects on other categories. Between-category complements (items bought alongside, like the halo of a promoted razor on blades) added about 20%, and between-category substitutes lost about 11%, for a net spillover of about 9% of the promoted item's own effect. In their data, category expansion was the largest part (72%), effects on other items in the same category 22% and stockpiling only 6%. Their conclusion was that cross-category effects are real but usually small and few were statistically significant, so looking within the category is often enough. For a store: credit a promotion with the extra margin on add-ons bought in the same orders, and debit it for sales lost by related items, but do not expect the halo to rescue a promotion that loses money on its own item. How to apply: in the promotion window, compare units of the top 10 co-purchased items (from basket analysis) with their forecast, and add or subtract the gap in your promotion P&L.
conditions: Stores running promotions on items with clear complements or substitutes in other categories.
fails_when: The promoted item has no regular complements, or the promotion targets new customers whose baskets differ from your base.

claim: Across four store datasets, about a third of a promotion's extra sales came from other brands' items, a third from other weeks (pull-forward) and a third from new category demand.
body: Van Heerde, Leeflang and Wittink split the short-term promotion spike into three parts: cross-brand (shoppers switching from other items), cross-period (purchases moved from the weeks before or after) and category expansion (genuinely new consumption). Each contributed about one third on average. Feature-supported discounts were strongly tied to cross-period effects, display-only deals to category expansion, and as discounts deepened the category-expansion share rose while switching and pull-forward shares fell. Extensions split switching into cannibalisation of the same brand's other items and switching between brands. For a single-brand store, the cross-brand third maps mostly to your own range. What it means for forecasting: never feed a raw promotion week into baseline history, and expect a dip after promotions as pulled-forward demand is repaid. What it means for judging a promotion: incremental units are the spike minus the post-promo dip minus what your other SKUs lost in the same weeks.
conditions: Brands that run price promotions on part of the range and want to forecast baseline demand or judge promo profit.
fails_when: Durable or one-time purchases where shoppers rarely stockpile, or new-customer promotions where most buyers are outside the existing base.

claim: Judge a line extension on net demand: its sales minus what it takes from your own range, which can be far below its total sales; measure it against a forecast of the existing SKUs.
body: Van Heerde, Srinivasan and Dekimpe built a model that splits a new product's sales into sources: shoppers new to the category, customers taken from competitors, and cannibalisation of the firm's own products. Applied to the Lexus RX300, the first crossover SUV, which could draw from both Lexus's luxury SUVs and its sedans, they show net demand may be considerably less than total demand, and that the mix of sources shifts over time. A store can run a simple version with its own data. Steps: 1) before launch, forecast the next 12 weeks for the SKUs most likely to lose sales (same use, same price band, same audience); 2) after launch, compare their actual sales with that forecast; 3) cannibalised units are the shortfall; 4) net incremental units are the new SKU's units minus that shortfall; 5) judge on contribution margin: new SKU margin minus margin lost on cannibalised units, minus the extra stock, photography and inventory risk. Recheck at week 12, since sources shift as the novelty fades.
conditions: Brands adding a variant, size, flavour or adjacent product that targets customers who already buy from them.
fails_when: Existing SKUs had stockouts or promotions in the comparison weeks, which breaks the forecast baseline; or the launch is mainly sold to new channels.

claim: Lift inflates rare pairs: a pair bought together in 20 of 1,000 orders scored lift 4.08 while one in 880 scored 1.02, so set a minimum support count before ranking bundle ideas by lift.
body: Lift divides observed co-purchase by what chance predicts, and when both items are rare, chance predicts a tiny number, so a handful of joint orders produces a big ratio. The textbook's Table 5.12 shows two pairs from 1,000 transactions: one pair bought together 880 times scores lift 1.02, while its mirror image, bought together only 20 times, scores 4.08, ranking the rare pair as four times more related. The cosine-style IS measure ranks them the opposite way (0.93 against 0.29), because it rewards pairs that are both frequent and linked. For a store this is the classic trap of bundling two slow SKUs that happened to appear together in a few orders. How to apply: first drop pairs with fewer than about 30 joint orders (or under 0.5% support in large stores), then rank the rest by lift, and check that the top pairs still make sense with IS or simple counts. Test a bundle as a page or offer before buying stock for it.
conditions: Stores mining order data for bundles, add-ons or cross-sell placements.
fails_when: The order file is small enough that even common pairs have few joint orders; widen the date range first.
numbers: 20 joint orders of 1,000: lift 4.08
880 joint orders of 1,000: lift 1.02
example floor: 30 joint orders or 0.5% support

claim: Rank add-on and bundle pairs by lift, not confidence: tea-to-coffee had 75% confidence yet lift 0.94 because 80% of everyone bought coffee, while tea-to-honey had 50% confidence but lift 4.2.
body: Definitions: support of A and B is the share of all orders containing both; confidence of A to B is the share of orders with A that also contain B; lift is confidence divided by the share of all orders containing B (equivalently, support of both divided by support of A times support of B). Lift 1 means no link, above 1 bought together more than chance, below 1 less. The textbook's tea and coffee example shows why confidence misleads: 75% of tea drinkers drink coffee, which looks strong, but 80% of all people drink coffee, so knowing someone drinks tea makes coffee slightly less likely (lift 0.75 / 0.80 = 0.94). Tea and honey looks weak at 50% confidence, yet only 12% of people use honey, so tea lifts honey use about fourfold (0.50 / 0.12 = 4.2). In a store, your bestseller appears in so many orders that it gets high confidence with everything. How to apply: export order lines, count pairs, compute all three measures, and pick bundle and 'frequently bought together' pairs with lift above about 1.5 and enough support.
conditions: Stores with enough multi-item orders to count pairs, roughly a few thousand orders.
fails_when: Most orders contain one item, or one product dominates orders, so pair counts are too small to trust.

tea to honey: confidence 50%, honey base 12%, lift about 4.2

claim: Rank SKUs by profit after complexity costs, not revenue: at one manufacturer 21% of products made 380% of profit while the other 79% destroyed 280%, and selective cuts lifted profit 25%.
body: Revenue-based ABC (as in Shopify's report) hides the cost of variety: extra setups, storage, working capital, slow-stock write-downs and overhead grow with the number of SKUs but are rarely charged to the SKUs that cause them. Innosight's whale curve plots cumulative profit, after allocating these complexity costs, against SKUs ranked from most to least profitable. The curve rises above 100% and then falls back. In one facility, 21% of products were profitable and produced 380% of total profit; the remaining 79%, carrying 19% of volume, destroyed 280%. Removing unprofitable SKUs selectively, rather than with a single margin cut-off, improved profit by 25%. For a store: per SKU, take contribution after landed cost, fees, fulfilment and returns; then charge each SKU a share of storage (by cubic volume and months held), photography and listing upkeep, and stock write-downs. Sort and plot cumulative profit. Candidates to cut sit on the falling tail, but check basket roles before cutting.
conditions: Ranges where SKUs differ a lot in volume, storage space, return rates or handling effort.
fails_when: Tail SKUs are add-ons that lift baskets for hero products, or entry items that win first orders, so their standalone profit understates their value.

79% of products (19% of volume) = -280% of profit
selective removal: +25% profit
